quote: One expresses the declaration that an object $a$ is an element of the \emph{type} $X$ by writing $a:X$.
note: This is notation for the typing judgment. In Narya, a : X is the native judgment.

quote: The \emph{type} of the function $x \mapsto e$ is called a \emph{product type} and will be denoted by $\prod_{x:X} T(x)$.
note: This is the native Narya Π-type (x : X) → T x. The non-dependent case is the native function type.

quote: the name of the variable no longer matters, in other words, that $x \mapsto e(x)$ and $t \mapsto e(t)$ may regarded as identical.
note: This is the alpha-equivalence of bound variables. The proof assistant handles it. It is not a statement.

quote: yielding $e(\blank)$ as alternative notation for the function $x \mapsto e(x)$.
note: This is the underscore notation for anonymous functions. It is only notation.

quote: The notation $b \jdeq c$ will denote the statement that the expressions $b$ and $c$ become the same thing …
note: This is the meta-level definitional equality (and \defeq for definitions). It corresponds to the judgmental equality of Narya. It is not an internal statement.

quote: We define the \emph{composite} function $g \circ f : X \to Z$ by setting $g \circ f \defeq (a \mapsto g(f(a)))$.
note: The formalization defines compose A B C g f ≔ x ↦ g (f x), as printed in the book.

quote: Then $(h \circ g) \circ f$ and $h \circ (g \circ f)$ are the same by definition
note: It is judgmental in Narya. Module 287 records it as a refl-typed check.

quote: $f \circ \id_X$ is the same by definition as $a \mapsto f(a)$, which … is to be regarded as the same as $f$.
note: f ∘ id ≡ f and id ∘ f ≡ f hold by eta. Module 287 records them as refl-typed checks.

quote: There are some types called \emph{universes}. … If $X$ is a type, then it appears as an element in some universe $\UU$.
note: Narya has one Type : Type. The formalization models a universe as a small-predicate with closure fields. It also has nested pairs U : U' with cumulativity. There is no hierarchy U_0 : U_1 : … and no designated smallest U_0.

quote: It follows from the properties above that there are an infinite number of universes, for each one is an element of a larger one.
note: This is a metatheoretic claim about the ambient hierarchy. Narya has Type : Type (total_universe contains its own type). Thus a faithful statement of the claim is not possible.

quote: The flexibility offered by this correspondence between families of types in $\UU$ and functions to $\UU$ will often be used.
note: This is native. Type families are functions X → Type. In the model, universe-restricted families are PropU/UniverseType-valued maps.

quote: Here are Peano's rules for constructing the natural numbers in the form that is used in type theory.
note: Nat is a native inductive type with judgmental computation. The rule (P4) is nat_ind.

quote: that different natural numbers have different successors; and that no number has $0$ as its successor. Those omitted rules remain true
note: The formalization proves two facts: the injectivity of successor (as an equivalence of path types) and 0 ≠ suc n.

quote: the difference between an induction principle and the corresponding recursion principle is that in the latter principle the type family is constant.
note: This is terminology only.

quote: We define by induction on $\NN$ the $m$-fold \emph{iteration} $e^m : Y \to Y$ by setting $e^0 \defeq \id_Y$ and $e^{\Succ(m)}\defeq e\circ e^m$.
note: The formalization has iterate A f (suc k) a = f (iterate A f k a). In the notation of the book, this is e^{S m} = e ∘ e^m, as printed.

quote: we define $n+m : \NN$ by induction on $\NN$ with respect to the variable $m$ by setting $n+0\defeq n$ and $n+\Succ(m)\defeq \Succ(n+m)$.
note: The function add recurses on its second argument, as printed in the book. The example 2+2 ≡ 4 holds judgmentally, but the formalization does not record it.

quote: we define the product $m \cdot n : \NN$ by induction on $m$ … $ \Succ(m) \cdot n \defeq (m \cdot n) + n$.
note: The function mul recurses on its second argument (m·S k = m·k + m). Thus the book's m·n is literally mul n m. The lemma mul_comm identifies the two orders.

quote: Alternatively (and equivalently) we may use iteration of functions to define addition and multiplication, by setting $n+m \defeq \Succ^m(n)$ …
note: Module 287 proves add n m = suc^m(n) and mul n m (the book's m·n) = (i ↦ i+n)^m(0) by nat_ind on m.

quote: we may define the factorial function $\fact : \NN \to \NN$ … setting $\fact(0) \defeq 1$ and $\fact(\Succ(m)) \defeq \Succ(m) \cdot \fact(m)$.
note: The function factorial (module 175) follows the printed recursion. The formalization does not record the check fact(3) ≡ 6.

quote: Here are the rules for constructing and using identity types.
note: The formalization uses the native HOTT Id, with J constructed in vendor J.ny. The computation rule of (E3) holds only as an identification. This is a documented foundation difference.

quote: moreover, if $X$ is an element of a universe $\UU$, then so is $a \eqto b$.
note: This is the field id_small of the universe model (module 190).

quote: We will refer to an element $i$ of $a \eqto b$ as an \emph{identification} of $a$ with $b$
note: This is terminology only.

quote: we will refer to an element $i$ of $a \eqto a$ as a \emph{symmetry} of $a$.
note: This is terminology for loops Id A a a. No separate declaration is necessary.

quote: Consider the identity type $\fact(2) \eqto 2$ … so we see from rule \ref{E2} that $\refl{\Succ(\Succ(0))}$ serves as an element of it.
note: Module 287 proves fact(2) = 2 and fact(3) = 6 by refl.

quote: We will see later that numbers only have trivial symmetries
note: ℕ is a set. The proof uses encode–decode.

quote: we may use concatenation to define powers $p^n : a \eqto a$ by induction on $n:\NN$; we set $p^0\defeq\refl{a}$ and $p^{n+1}\defeq p\cdot p^n$.
note: The formalization has loop_power_nat (n+1) = concat (p^n) p, that is, p·p^n in book notation. The declaration loop_power extends this to Int with p^{-n} = (p^{-1})^n, as in the text and the footnote.

quote: The transport functions behave as expected: we may construct an identification of type $\trp {e'\circ e} \eqto \trp {e'} \circ \trp {e}$.
note: The formalization restates this as xca:trp-compose.

quote: Take, for example, $T(x)\defeq (x \eqto x)$. Then $\trp e$ … transports a symmetry of $a$ to a symmetry of $b$.
note: The formalization computes transport in the loop family as conjugation (xca:trp-in-a/x=b/x).

quote: If $X$ and $Y(x)$ are elements of a universe $\UU$, then so is $\prod_{x:X} Y(x)$.
note: This is the field pi_small of the universe model (module 190).

quote: we may abbreviate $\ap{f,x,x'}$ by writing $\ap{f}$ instead. For convenience, we may abbreviate it even further, writing $f(p)$
note: This is notation. The book also uses it for apd and apap. Narya writes refl f p / map_path.

quote: The functions provided by these two definitions are not equal by definition, but they can be identified
note: In Narya, happly p x is definitionally ap_{ev_x}(p). Module 287 records this by refl.

quote: Similarly, one can define the inverse of a path over a path, writing $\inv q : \pathover {y'} Y {\inv p} y$
note: Module 17 defines it with the typal reflexivity law.

quote: For these operations on paths over paths we have identifications analogous to those for the operations on paths in \cref{xca:path-groupoid-laws}, after some modification.
note: This covers all six laws. Each law lies over the corresponding base law (module 281, xca:cp).

quote: There are \emph{sums} of types. … $\sum _{x:X} Y(x)$ whose elements are all pairs $(a,b)$, where $a:X$ and $b:Y(a)$.
note: This is the native Narya Σ with the fields fst/snd. These fields are the projections of lines 1125–1133.

quote: If $X$ and $Y(x)$ are elements of a universe $\UU$, then so is $\sum _{x:X} Y(x)$.
note: This is the field sigma_small of the universe model (module 190).

quote: By path composition, one sees that any element $x : X$ can serve as the center of a contraction of a contractible type $X$.
note: Module 287 gives a contraction centred at any x. The proof uses path composition.

quote: Using $t$ we can define an inverse function $g : Y \to X$ by setting $g(y)\defeq\fst(\fst(t(y)))$.
note: The map equiv_inverse_map is e .equiv b .center .fst, that is, fst(fst(t(y))). The two inverse laws of lines 1248–1258 are equiv_counit and equiv_retraction.

quote: For any type $X$, the identity function $\id_X$ is an equivalence from $X$ to $X$.
note: The proof is as in the text: the fibers of the identity are singletons.

quote: the function $\trp[T]{e}$ from \cref{def:transport} is an equivalence from $T(x)$ to $T(y)$, for all $e: x \eqto y$.
note: The formalization states transport_equiv for paths in the universe. The family case is its instance at ap_T(e) = refl T e. The map of this instance is transport in T. There is no dedicated family-level declaration.

quote: First, we use \cref{lem:weq-iso} to construct an element of … i.e., the associativity of sum types
note: This is footnote ft:Sigma-assoc. The declaration sigma_assoc is the associativity equivalence with refl inverse laws.

quote: Then, we construct for any contractible type $X$ and for any family of types $Y(x)$ … an equivalence between $\sum_{x:X}Y(x)$ and $Y(c)$
note: Module 287 proves Σ_{x:X} Y(x) ≃ Y(c) for contractible X. The proof uses Y(x) ≃ (c = x) × Y(x) and contract_away_simple.

quote: The special case $Z\jdeq X$, $f\jdeq\id_X$ applies to any product type.
note: This is a direct instance at f = id. The formalization does not state it separately.

quote: will be treated transparently, \ie we will pass between $f(x,y)$ and $f(x)(y)$ without denoting it.
note: The formalization always passes explicitly through curry_equiv or pattern matching.

quote: We often use $\fst(\pathpair p q) \eqto p$ and $\snd(\pathpair p q) \eqto q$ … Similarly, $r \eqto \pathpair {\fst(r)}{\snd(r)}$ by induction on $r$.
note: The formalization records this under lem:isEq-pair=. For native Id, all of it is judgmental.

quote: There is special case of sum types that deserves to be mentioned … the sum type is called the \emph{binary product}
note: The formalization defines Product A B ≔ Σ A (_ ↦ B), exactly as described (also rem:non-dependent-sums).

quote: There is an equivalence between $(a_1,b_1) \eqto (a_2,b_2)$ and $(a_1 \eqto a_2) \times (b_1 \eqto b_2)$.
note: This is also lem:isEq-pair-bin=.

quote: we let $f\times f'$ denote the map of type $(X\times X') \to (Y\times Y')$ that sends $(x,x')$ to $(f(x),f'(x'))$.
note: The formalization defines f × f′ in general. By refl, product_equiv's map is f × f′. Also, f × f′ is an equivalence when f and f′ are equivalences (module 287).

quote: we may prove that any two elements $x$ and $y$ of $\emptytype$ are equal … by using induction on $x$
note: Ex falso is absurd. The lemma empty_prop gives that any two elements are equal.

quote: to assert that a type $T$ has no elements … Providing a function of type $T \to \emptytype$ is a convenient way
note: The formalization defines Not A ≔ A → Empty.

quote: we may construct, for any element $u : \true$, an identification of type $u \eqto \triv$ … for any elements $x$ and $y$ of $\true$
note: The lemma unit_prop gives u = star and x = y for all elements of Unit. The proof uses induction, as in the text.

quote: We may use substitution to construct an element of type $(\yes \eqto \no)\to \emptytype$
note: The term bool_encode true. false. has the type Id Bool true false → Empty, because BoolCode true false ≡ Empty (the book's P). There is no separately named lemma.

quote: The definition of $P(b)$ is motivated by the expectation that we will be able to construct an equivalence between $P(b)$ and $\yes \eqto b$.
note: Module 287 proves (true = b) ≃ BoolCode true b. Here BoolCode true is the book's P.

quote: we may use substitution to prove that it is absurd that successors of natural numbers are identical to $0$
note: The lemma nat_zero_ne_suc is nat_encode at (0, suc n). Its code NatCode 0 (suc n) is Empty (the book's P).

quote: The definition of $P(i)$ is motivated by the expectation that we will be able to construct an equivalence between $P(i)$ and $0 \eqto i$.
note: Module 287 proves (0 = i) ≃ NatCode 0 i. Here NatCode 0 is the book's P.

quote: The \emph{binary sum} of two types $X$ and $Y$, denoted $X \amalg Y$, is an inductive type with two constructors
note: This is a native data type with the constructors inl./inr.

quote: Thus $\inl{x} \eqto \inr{y}$ is always empty, and there are equivalences of type $(\inl{x} \eqto \inl{x'}) \equivto (x \eqto x')$
note: This covers all four constructor combinations (xca:binary-sum-id).

quote: The \emph{unary sum} or \emph{wrapped copy} of $X$ is an inductive type $\Copy(X)$ … with a single constructor
note: The function copy_value is the destructor out.

quote: Note that $\Copy(X)$ can alternatively be defined as $\sum_{z:\true}X$.
note: Module 287 proves Copy(X) ≃ Σ_{z:1} X.

quote: the induction principle implies that $\inc{\out(z)} \eqto z$ for all $z:\Copy(X)$, so there is an equivalence of type $\Copy(X) \equivto X$
note: The formalization builds copy_equiv from copy_value (out). It proves inc(out z) = z by induction on z, as in the text.

quote: It follows that there are equivalences of type $(\inc{x} \eqto \inc{x'}) \equivto (x \eqto x')$ and $(\out(z) \eqto \out(z')) \equivto (z \eqto z')$.
note: These are instances of map_equiv_to_paths at copy_equiv and at its inverse. The lemma map_equiv_to_paths states that ap of an equivalence is an equivalence. The formalization does not state the instances separately.

quote: we can make several copies of $X$ that are not equal to each other by definition, for instance, by picking different names for the constructor.
note: This is about the definitional distinctness of data types. For example, NegNat (exa:nnn) is a separate data type.

quote: we can define a function $\len : X^* \to \NN$, giving the length of a list, satisfying $\len(\varepsilon) \jdeq 0$ and $\len(x\ell) \jdeq \Succ(\len(\ell))$.
note: The function length follows the printed recursion: 0 on nil, suc on cons.

quote: there are no general functions producing the head and tail of an arbitrary list, since the empty list has neither head nor tail.
note: There is no map (X : Type) → X* → X (take X = ∅). The type ε = x t is empty. The functions hd and tl have the book's computation rules by definition (module 287).

quote: We shall see in~\cref{thm:isset-inductive-types} below that $X^*$ is a set whenever $X$ is.
note: This is a forward reference to thm:isset-inductive-types. The lemma list_set takes isSet A.

quote: We may write $\trp[\id_\UU]{p}$ more briefly as $\ptoe p$, which we also use to denote the corresponding function of type $X\to Y$
note: The underlying map of transport_equiv A B p is p .trr.

quote: Thus there are identifications of type $\etop {\ptoe p} \eqto p$ and $\ptoe {\etop f} \eqto f$.
note: The formalization has both inverse laws of ua with the exact transport map.

quote: There are also identifications of type $\overetop{\id_X} \eqto \refl{X}$ and $\overetop{g\,f} \eqto \etop{g}\,\etop{f}$ if $g: Y\equivto Z$.
note: The lemma ua_compose states ua(d∘e) = ua e · ua d in concatenation order. In book notation, this is etop(g)etop(f).

quote: An important special case … $\trp[X \mapsto (X\to X)]{\etop g} (f) \eqto g\circ f \circ g^{-1}$.
note: The formalization proves it as an identification of functions. It is listed under lem:trp-in-function-type.

quote: We shall call a type $P$ with that property a \emph{proposition}, and its elements will be called \emph{proofs} of $P$.
note: The formalization defines isProp A ≔ (x y : A) → Id A x y, as in the text. The formal version is at def:isSet.

quote: Then English phrases such as ``$P$ holds'', ``we know $P$'', and ``we have shown $P$'', will all mean that we have an element of $P$.
note: This is a reading convention for prose.

quote: If for any $x:X$ and any $y:X$ the identity type $x \eqto y$ is a proposition, then we shall say that $X$ is a \emph{set}.
note: This is also called a 0-type. Its HLevel index is 2.

quote: Some authors therefore call propositions \emph{$(-1)$-types}, and they call contractible types \emph{$(-2)$-types}.
note: HLevel index k is book level k−2. Index 0 is the contractible types, 1 is the propositions and 2 is the sets.

quote: Equations are propositions, so we can speak of them being true or false
note: Equation packages Id with the proof that Id is a proposition. This proof comes from the set.

quote: If for any $x:X$ and any $y:X$ the identity type $x \eqto y$ is a set, then we shall say that $X$ is a \emph{groupoid}
note: This is also called a 1-type. Its HLevel index is 3.

quote: If for any $n:\NN$, any $x:X$, and any $y:X$ the identity type $x \eqto y$ is an $n$-\emph{type} … $X$ is an $(n+1)$-\emph{type}.
note: HLevel is the same recursion, shifted by 2. It starts from contractibility. The term 'n-truncated' names the same notion.

quote: We prove that every proposition is a set, from which it follows by induction that every $n$-type is an $(n+1)$-\emph{type}.
note: The lemma prop_is_set is lem:prop-is-set. The lemma hlevel_raise is the induction step for every level.

quote: Since $\false$ is a proposition, it follows by \ref{prop-utils-codom} above that $A\to\emptytype$ is a proposition for any type $A$.
note: The lemma negation_prop proves isProp (A → Empty) for an arbitrary type A.

quote: $\true\amalg \true$ has two distinct elements $\inl{\triv}$ and $\inr{\triv}$, an is therefore \emph{not} a proposition.
note: Module 287 proves inl(triv) ≠ inr(triv). Thus 1 ⨿ 1 (and Bool) is not a proposition.

quote: Similarly, $\sum_{n:\NN} \true$ has infinitely many distinct elements $(n,\triv)$ and is not a proposition.
note: Module 287 shows that n ↦ (n,triv) reflects paths. It also shows that Σ_{n:ℕ} 1 is not a proposition.

quote: we will use identifiers starting with ``is'' only for names of types that are propositions. Examples are … and also $\isEq(f)$.
note: This is a naming convention. The formalization proves its one non-trivial instance: isEq is a proposition.

quote: the inductive definition of $n$-types can indeed start with $n$ as $-2$, where we have the contractible types.
note: HLevel starts at index 0 = isContr. The exercise xca:prop-contractible= links the levels.

quote: any function $g: T\to P$ to a proposition $P$ yields a (unique) function $f:\Trunc{T}\to P$ satisfying $f(\trunc{t})\jdeq g(t)$
note: For native Mere, the computation is judgmental. Uniqueness follows from the universal property.

quote: for any proposition $P$, precomposition with $\trunc{\_}$ is an equivalence of type $(\Trunc{T} \to P) \equivto (T \to P)$.
note: The _book_map companion states that precomposition itself is the equivalence.

quote:
the concept of $T$ \emph{not being empty}, which would be represented by the proposition $
eg(T \eqto \emptytype)$, which is equivalent to $
eg
eg T$.
note: The lemma not_empty_double_negation is an equivalence ¬(T = Empty) ≃ ¬¬T for arbitrary T. The proof uses ua.

quote: let $\Trunc \blank$ have the type $\UU\to\sum_{X:\UU}\isprop(X)$. The type $\sum_{X:\UU}\isprop(X)$ is also denoted as $\Prop_\UU$
note: Universe closure under truncation is the model field trunc_small.

quote: It will turn out that $A_{(a)}$ is a subtype of $A$.
note: The component is a Σ over the proposition-valued family ‖a = x‖.

quote: Note that the empty type $\emptytype$ is \emph{not} connected.
note: Module 287 proves that ∅ is not connected, for every truncation signature.

quote: Consider the function $f:\bn{1}\to\bn{2}$ that is constant $0$. … Hence $f$ is not an equivalence.
note: This is about the constant-0 map 1 → 2 (module 287). Its fiber at 1 is empty, so the map is not an equivalence. All fibers of the map are propositions.

quote: As a function between sets $f$ is an injection (one-to-one), but not a surjection.
note: The constant-0 map 1 → 2 is an injection and not a surjection (module 287).

quote: This is equivalent to saying we have a function $g:B\to A$ and an identification $p: f\circ g \eqto \id_B$
note: This is a footnote of def:surjection (module 280).

quote: This argument applies generally: Any non-empty proposition is contractible.
note: A non-empty proposition is contractible, for every truncation signature (module 287).

quote: If the types $A$ and $B$ in the above lemma are \emph{sets}, then we call equivalences between $A$ and $B$ also \emph{bijections}.
note: This is terminology only.

quote: each $\ap{f}$ is an equivalence if and only if all implications … hold, but this is in general not sufficient.
note: This is a footnote of lem:inj-ap (module 280). Only B must be a set.

quote: Note that $(\exists_{x:A}(y \eqto f(x))) \jdeq \Trunc{f^{-1}(y)}$ … For this reason, $\im(f)$ is called the \emph{propositional} image.
note: The formalization defines Image with Mere of the book fiber. Thus this holds by definition.

quote: This diagram actually commutes by definition.
note: The term image_triangle is refl f.

quote: Thus the image factorization of $f$ is a 6-tuple. … as do the proofs that $g$ is an injection and $h$ is a surjection.
note: ImageFactorizations is the 6-tuple. The margin note swaps the roles: the displayed type has issurj(g), isinj(h). This is a typo in the book.

quote: with the Law of Excluded Middle, one can derive $P$ from the latter
note: The proof is by contradiction under LEM (also xca:dne-lem).

quote: The map $P\mapsto P$ is welltyped by \emph{cumulativity} of the universes … Note that the map is not the identity function due to its type.
note: Cumulativity is the model field of NestedUniverses. The map is prop_inclusion.

quote: Note that $\sum_{X:\UU}(A \equivto X)$, the type expressing that $A$ is essentially $\UU$-small, is a proposition by the univalence axiom for $\UU$.
note: The formalization proves essentially_small_prop from univalence. The proof uses the contractibility of Σ X, A ≃ X.

quote: Of course, any $A:\UU$ is essentially $\UU$-small, and any essentially $\UU$-small type is locally $\UU$-small.
note: Module 190 proves both implications for every universe of the model.

quote: To show that a type is locally $\UU$-small we have to give a reflexive relation … that induces, by path induction, a family of equivalences
note: This covers both directions of the criterion.

quote: This follows from our replacement principle, assuming propositional resizing, or the even stronger principle of the excluded middle.
note: This is a comparison with set-theoretic replacement. The development has no set-theoretic model. The pri:replacement note records this as informal.

quote: The replacement principle can be proved using the join construction of the image … assumption that the universes are closed under pushouts.
note: The join-construction proof needs pushouts (higher inductive types). Narya does not have them. The formalization uses replacement only as a hypothesis.

quote: Another consequence is that the type of finite sets, which we'll define below in~\cref{def:groupoidFin}, is essentially small.
note: The formal statement assumes replacement.

quote: In this section, we give two (equivalent) definitions of the notion of a subtype of a given type $T$.
note: This is lem:Sub(T)=Inj(T).

quote: Note that giving a predicate on $T$ is equivalent to giving a map $Q: T\to\Prop_\UU$ for a suitable universe $\UU$
note: By definition, predicates are PropTypes-valued (or PropU-valued) maps.

quote: we can form the predicate $P(t)\defeq (f(t) \eq \yes)$ … However, not every predicate can be given through a $f: T\to\bool$
note: P is given through f when P = (t ↦ f(t) = yes) in T → Prop. Such an f is unique, and it exists if and only if P is decidable. Every predicate on every type is given in this way if and only if LEM holds (an equivalence of propositions). Module 287 proves these facts.

quote: we can define $\chi_P: T\to\bool$ … In this way, decidable predicates on a type $T$ correspond to their characteristic functions $T\to\bool$.
note: Module 287 proves that P ↦ χ_P is an equivalence DecidablePredicate T ≃ (T → Bool) (BookIsEquiv of χ). Its inverse is f ↦ (f(–) = yes).

quote: \cref{cor:contract-away} gives that $\inv\fst(t)\weq P(t)$ for all $t:T$, so that $\fst$ is an injection.
note: This also covers line 3416: (T_P, fst) is an injection into T.

quote: Since $\Prop$ is a set, $\Sub(T)$ is also a set, for any type $T$.
note: The lemma subtypes_set is pi_set over propositions_set (lem:Prop-in-Set), as in the text.

quote: The identity types $P\eq_{\Sub(T)} Q$ and $T_P\eqto_{\UU} T_Q$ are in general not equivalent!
note: Module 287 gives the counterexample T = Bool, P = (– = true), Q = (– = false). Here T_P = T_Q (both are contractible), but P ≠ Q. Thus there is no equivalence (P = Q) ≃ (T_P = T_Q). Also, there is no such family for all T, P, Q.

quote: As a consequence, $\Inj(T)$ is a set since $\Sub(T)$ is, for any type $T$.
note: The lemma injections_into_set is also listed under cor:Inj(T)-is-set.

quote: we have universes, and the identity type of $\Inj^\UU(T)$ identifies precisely the triples defining the same subset.
note: Module 287 shows that paths in Inj(T) are paths of the fiber predicates. Equivalently, they are pointwise equivalences of the fibers.

quote: we then call $T_P$ a \emph{subset} of $T$ and we may denote it by $\setof{t:T}{P(t)}$.
note: SubtypeCarrier T P is Σ T (t ↦ P t .fst). This is the book's T_P.

quote: Any proposition has decidable identity types … and is thus a \emph{decidable set}, even though it may not be \emph{decidable as a proposition}.
note: The formalization states proposition_decidable_set for any proposition. The contrast with the decidability of P itself needs no statement.

quote: The way we phrased this definition implies that $A$ is a set.
note: The lemma decidable_set_is_set extracts sethood from the proposition clause of the definition.

quote: Therefore the following is \emph{not} a subtype of $\UU$.
note: The map fst : U_* → U is not even 0-truncated: its fiber over Set is not a set. Hence it is not an injection. The formalization does not state the subtype corollary separately.

quote: In particular, $(gf)_\div \jdeq g_\div f_\div$.
note: This holds by the definition of book_pointed_compose.

quote: The following lemma holds for $n$-types in general, but we only need it for propostions and sets.
note: For all levels, X ≃ Y is an n-type when Y is an n-type. Also, the type of n-types is an (n+1)-type.

quote: One may wonder whether $\NN$ … is a set. The answer is yes, but it is harder to prove than one would think.
note: The proof of nat_set uses encode–decode, not Hedberg.

quote: A variation can be used to give a complete characterization of the identity types of inductive types.
note: The formalization characterizes the identity types of 1, Bool, ℕ, Copy (module 287), sums and lists by equivalences.

quote: For lists, this gives equivalences … we can deduce more generally that $X^*$ is an $n$-type, when $X$ is an $n$-type
note: The formalization records this under thm:isset-inductive-types.

quote: for any set $S$ and any function $g: T\to S$ there is a (unique) function $f:\Trunc{T}_0\to S$ satisfying $f(\trunc{t}_0)\jdeq g(t)$
note: The non-dependent computation holds definitionally.

quote: Lemma~7.3.12 gives an equivalence from $\trunc{t}_0 \eq \trunc{t'}_0$ to $\Trunc{t \eqto t'}$
note: For the quotient construction of SetTrunc, set_trunc_paths gives (|t|₀ = |t'|₀) ≃ ‖t = t'‖.

quote: for any set $S$, precomposition with $\trunc{\_}_0$ is an equivalence … This is called \emph{the universal property of set truncation}.
note: The lemma set_trunc_universal_property states that precomposition with set_trunc is an equivalence for every set S.

quote: More generally, there are operations turning any type into an $n$-type … with constant truncation operator $\Trunc{T}_{-2}\defeq\true$
note: Module 285 defines ‖T‖_{−2} ≔ 1 and |t|_{−2} ≔ triv. This is a (−2)-type with the universal property (module 287): precomposition with |–|_{−2} is an equivalence into every (−2)-type.

quote: This is in contrast to a \emph{constant} map … Any constant map is indeed weakly constant.
note: Module 287 proves that constant maps are weakly constant. Maps identified with a constant map are also weakly constant.

quote: Note also that when $B$ is a set, weak constancy of $f : A \to B$ is a proposition.
note: This is also listed with the unnumbered definition at 3862.

quote: The key point is that $\im(f)$ is a proposition because $f$ is weakly constant.
note: The lemma weakly_constant_image_prop proves that the image of a weakly constant map into a set is a proposition.

quote: $(\Succ(w),\Succ(d))$, for example, determines the same net worth as $(w,d)$, and $(\Succ(w),\Succ(d))\ne(w,d)$.
note: Module 287 proves Succ(w) + d = w + Succ(d) and (Succ(w),Succ(d)) ≠ (w,d).

quote: Recall that an \emph{equivalence relation} is one that is (1) \emph{reflexive} … (2) \emph{symmetric} … (3) \emph{transitive}
note: This is a proposition-valued relation with the three laws.

quote: the equivalence relation is $R((w_1,d_1),(w_2,d_2)) \defeq  (w_1+d_2 = w_2 + d_1)$, precisely capturing equality of net worth
note: The declaration balance_relation packages SameBalance with its reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity (same_balance_trans).

quote: the type $A/R$ could in fact be used as a type of integers

note: This is a footnote of def:quotient-set. It covers both routes: replacement and resizing.

quote: Note that $R\mapsto(z\mapsto R(\fst(z))(\snd(z))$ is an equivalence from $A\to(A\to\Prop)$ to $(A\times A)\to\Prop)$.
note: This is an instance of curry_equiv.

quote: Any element of the image of $R$ is merely an equivalence predicate
note: This holds by the definition of Quotient as Image. The second component is the truncated fiber. The formalization does not state the pointwise iff form separately.

quote: We will construct the center of contraction $\bar f : A/R \to B$ such that $\bar f([x]) \jdeq f(x)$ for all $x:A$.

quote: Convince yourself that a general equivalence relation on a finite set looks like a union of such complete graphs.

note: The function nat_pred (module 07) is the printed two-clause definition.

quote: Elementary properties of addition, multiplication and predecessor can be proved in type theory in the usual way. We freely use them

quote: By Hedberg's \cref{thm:hedberg}, we get an alternate proof that $\NN$ is a set.
note: This is a direct application. The formalization does not state it as a named instance.

quote: First note that $P_{\min}(n)$ is a proposition, and that all $n$ such that $P_{\min}(n)$ are equal.
note: The lemmas isminimum_prop and minimum_unique (inside minimum_prop) give both remarks. The lemma minimum_prop shows that Σ n, P_min(n) is a proposition.

quote: we define a function $\mu_P:\NN\to\NN$ which, given input $n$, searches for a $k<n$ such that $P(k)$. … we will call \emph{bounded search}.
note: The book uses μ_P again in the proofs of lem:PHP and lem:euclid-div. The formal proofs of these lemmas use other arguments.

quote: $\mu_P(n)\leq n \quad\text{and}\quad \mu_P(n)<n \to P(\mu_P(n))$ … $P(m) \to \mu_P(n)\leq m$
note: This covers all displayed invariants of the implementation of def:Nwellordered.

quote: When moving beyond sets, there are two different ways in which a type can be finite: an \emph{additive} way and a \emph{multiplicative} way
note: The book does not define the additive and multiplicative notions of finiteness.

quote: Here it doesn't matter whether we take the sum over $\Set$ or over $\UU$, since any finite set is a set.
note: This is a footnote of def:groupoidFin. It includes the displayed chain of identifications.

quote: Observe that we have identifications in $\FinSet_0 \eqto \FinSet_1 \eqto \bn{1} $, and in $\FinSet \eqto \sum_{n:\NN}\FinSet_n$
note: All three identifications are paths in the universe (module 38 and def:groupoidFin).

quote: Also, $\FinSet$ is the image of the map $\Fin : \NN \to \UU$ … and is hence essentially $\UU$-small (for any universe $\UU$)
note: This assumes replacement. The declaration nat_small plays the role of 'U_0 is the smallest universe'.

quote: We have already seen several examples of 2-element sets: $\bool$, $\bn{2}$, $\bn{1}\amalg\bn{1}$ that can easily be identified.
note: Module 287 proves 1 ⨿ 1 ≃ 2 ≃ Bool.

quote: one cannot identify an \emph{arbitrary} 2-element set with any of these. … Having a name for one of the elements would be sufficient
note: This includes the footnote: a chosen point determines Bool ≃ A.

quote: We need $n\ge 0$, since for a contractible ($-2$-type) $X$ we get an equivalence $X^* \equivto \NN$ … and $\NN$ is not contractible.
note: ℕ is not contractible. Thus X* is not contractible for contractible X (module 287).

quote: If $f$ in \cref{lem:sum-of-fibers} is an injection, then … $A$ is a $n$-type if $B$ is a $n$-type
note: The lemma truncated_map_domain_hlevel transfers any h-level from B to A along a truncated map. Injections are (−1)-truncated maps.

quote: Note that we need $A$ to be in the same universe as the one we're taking type families in.
note: The universe-stratified version is small_families_maps_equiv (module 193).

quote: Since the type of $n$-types is an $(n+1)$-type, $\Trunc A_{n+1}$ is an $(n+1)$-type
note: The lemma ntypes_level states that NTypes k (types of h-level k+1) has h-level k+2. That is, the type of n-types is an (n+1)-type. The lemma trunc_step_level uses it.

quote: Since this is a proposition and $\trunc\blank_{n+1}$ is surjective
note: The lemma trunc_unit_surjective holds for every level k.

quote: Finally, we need to re-size $\Trunc A_{n+1}$ to fit in the universe $\UU$ that $A$ came from.
note: The formal statement assumes replacement.

quote: any map $f : B \to A$ can be described as ``projecting away'' its fibers, by using the equivalence $e$
note: This is lem:sum-of-fibers.

quote: If $A$ and $B$ are groupoids, these fibers are themselves groupoids
note: The formal statement is for every level.

quote: $f$ \emph{forgets at most structure} if all the fibers are sets; … \emph{forgets nothing} if all the fibers are contractible.
note: This is TruncatedMap at h-levels 2, 1 and 0.

quote: Of course, a map forgets properties if and only if it's an injection, and it forgets nothing if and only if it's an equivalence.
note: One equivalence is between a TruncatedMap level and IsEmbedding. The other is between a TruncatedMap level and BookIsEquiv.

quote: $f$ \emph{forgets at most $n$-structure} if all the fibers are $n$-truncated.
note: This also covers the terminology 1-structure (stuff), 0-structure and (−1)-structure.

quote: we can factor $f : B \to A$ through first its \emph{$0$-image} and then its usual $(-1)$-image
note: The formalization assembles the factorization A → ZeroImage → Image → B from modules 106, 39 and 164.

quote: we can define the $n$-image in a similar way and prove that the $n$-image factorization is unique.
note: This is in modules 230–232.

quote: Since the unit type $\bn 1$ is the unique $(-2)$-type, we have $\Trunc{X}_{-2} \eqto \bn 1$ for any type $X$.
note: Modules 285 and 287 prove three facts. Every (−2)-type is identified with 1. The type Σ_{X:Type} isContr X is contractible. Also, ‖X‖_{−2} ≃ 1.

quote: not only are the fibers sets, they are \emph{nonempty} sets … Note also that the fibers of the first map are connected
note: The last map is the embedding of the image. It forgets at most properties.

quote: a function 1 → A provides exactly the same information as picking an element in A
note: This is a Chapter-2 fact (xca:Xequiv1toX). The chapter introduction recalls it.

quote: a function A → Prop provides exactly the same information as picking a subtype of A
note: These are Chapter-2 facts (def:subtype, lem:Sub(T)=Inj(T)). The introduction recalls them.

quote: if there is an identification of type p = refl_a, then all the iterations of p can be identified with each other
note: Module 288 proves that if p = refl_a, then every power p^z is refl_a. Thus all iterations of p are identified with each other.

quote: f(base) :≡ a and f(loop) := l ... f(loop) and l are not equal by definition, but an identification is given
note: This is notation for circle recursion. In the project, even the base computation is an identification (README computation-rule policy).

quote: The inverse to ev_A^a sends l : a = a to (ve_A(a,l), refl_a). Try to verify this!
note: This is a footnote of cor:circle-loopspace. The formalization proves both inverse laws of the footnote recursor.

quote: having an element of type ∏_{z:S¹}(base = z) contradicts the univalence axiom
note: Module 288 shows that an element of ∏_z(base = z) makes S¹ contractible. Hence S¹ is a set, and circle_not_set refutes this.

quote: it also turns out that the type base = base is equivalent to the type x = x, for any x : S¹
note: This is a footnote. The equivalence circle_coordinate_loop_equiv is exactly (base = base) ≃ (x = x).

quote: The latter type [S¹ =_U S¹] is equivalent to S¹ ⊔ S¹, as follows from xca:S1=S1-components and xca:(S1->S1)_(f)-eqv-S1
note: This is the same statement as circle.tex:1211. The formalization proves it for every CircleSignature.

quote: alternatives: 2n/2n+1 in N; N ⊔ N; N ⊔ 1 ⊔ N; quotient of N×N; canonical-representative subset; loops base = base
note: Module 288 adds the parity encoding (2n ↦ n, 2n+1 ↦ −n−1). It also adds ℕ ⊔ ℕ in the book's labelling and ℕ ⊔ 1 ⊔ ℕ. Each of these has the decoding map as BookIsEquiv. The formalization already proves that the quotient, normal-form and loop encodings are equivalent to Int.

quote: we can leave out the constructor symbols ι± when the type is clear from context
note: This is a notational convention. The project writes the constructors pos./neg. explicitly.

quote: Like the type N, the type ℤ is a set with decidable equality and ordering relations.
note: The formalization proves all three properties for the native Int.

quote: negation −ι₊(n) :≡ ι₋(−n), −ι₋(m) :≡ ι₊(−m), ap₋(zeq) := zeq⁻¹
note: The definition uses pattern matching on the native Int.

quote: Negation is its own inverse.
note: The formalization proves the involution law pointwise and packages it as an equivalence.

quote: The successor function s is likewise defined inductively, setting s(n) :≡ succ(n), s(−0) :≡ 1, s(−succ(n)) :≡ −n
note: This is the native successor on Int.

quote: The successor function s is an equivalence.
note: The explicit inverse is int_pred, with both laws.

quote: The inverse of s is called the predecessor function ... this defines the iteration s^z for all z; likewise f^z for any equivalence f
note: The formalization defines signed iteration for any equivalence (module 57) and for loops (module 26).

quote: Addition of integers is now defined by iteration: z + y :≡ s^y(z) ... subtraction z − y :≡ z + (−y)
note: The function int_add is literally signed iteration of int_succ. The function int_sub is z + (−y).

quote: Since addition and subtraction are mutually inverse, the function w ↦ z + w is an equivalence
note: The formalization proves both inverse laws and the translation equivalence.

quote: we may iterate it to define multiplication: zy :≡ (w ↦ z + w)^y(0)
note: The function int_mul is literally signed iteration of translation. The iteration starts at 0.

quote: The ordering relations < and ≤ on ℤ are easily defined and shown to extend those on N.
note: The formalization shows that both relations agree with the book order on naturals.

quote: we will often give f(0) directly, and define g′ and h′ ... f(z+1) ≡ g′(z, f(z)) for all z ≥ 0
note: This is a derived induction principle with judgmental rules. Narya pattern matching on Int plays this role, but no declaration states it.

quote: Here it suffices that A is a pointed type ... the forgetful map Σ_b((A,a) →* (B,b)) → (A → B) is an equivalence
note: This is a footnote of def:covering. The formalization proves it with the actual forgetful map.

quote: SetBundle(B) :≡ Σ_{A:U} Σ_{f:A→B} ∏_{b:B} isset(f⁻¹(b)), with variations according to the flavor
note: This covers the type of coverings and its flavors, with book-oriented fibers.

quote: Recall the equivalence ... between B → Set and the type of coverings over B. We shall frequently use this equivalence, even without explicit mention.
note: This is the Chapter-2 lem:Set-families, repackaged for Coverings.

quote: all variations of coverings defined by a predicate are groupoids as well. This does not apply to pointed coverings
note: The formalization proves the predicate variants. The remark on pointed coverings says only that the argument does not apply. It carries no formal claim.

quote: A′ :≡ Σ_{z:S¹} Bool = (S¹ × Bool) = (S¹ + S¹), and the latter type is not connected
note: Module 288 proves Σ_{z:S¹} Bool ≡ S¹ × Bool (refl) ≃ S¹ + S¹. It also gives the displayed chain as an identification of types (ua). Finally, it proves that A + A is never connected.

quote: the left subtype diagram is fully general: it also holds when we replace S¹ by any type B. This is not true for the right
note: The formalization proves the left square for arbitrary B. The negative claim about the right diagram has no declaration. This claim needs a connected base.

quote: In slogan form: A covering over the circle is a set with a permutation of its elements.
note: This is a slogan for thm:coveringsofS1perms. Monodromy is transport along loop.

quote: In the above definition we get that h : A →* C is a covering as well by xca:covering-utils(left-cancel)
note: Let f and g be coverings. Module 288 proves that the h of every lift (h, f = gh) in PointedCoverLifts is a covering. The proof uses coverings_left_cancel.

quote: The examples preceding def:univ-cover are indeed universal coverings according to the following lemma.
note: This is the universality of the path covering and of the constant map from Fin 1 over any pointed groupoid.

quote: In the next section we will see that the exponential covering of the circle is in fact universal.
note: This is a forward reference to cor:univ-covers-S1.

quote: under this equivalence 0 corresponds to refl_base, 1 to loop, −1 to loop⁻¹; the successor corresponds to composition with loop
note: The formalization proves all compatibilities of the winding number for every CircleSignature.

quote: It follows directly that addition of integers corresponds to composition of loops.
note: This is a margin note.

quote: giving h(z) : P(z) → Q(z) for all z : S¹ is the same as h(base) with h(loop) : Q(loop) h(base) P(loop)⁻¹ = h(base)
note: Module 288 proves Π_z(P z → Q z) ≃ Σ_{h : P base → Q base}(Q(loop) ∘ h ∘ P(loop)⁻¹ = h). BookIsEquiv holds for the map h ↦ (h(base), h(loop)). When Q(base) is a set, the identification is the commuting square Q(loop) ∘ h = h ∘ P(loop) (line 994).

quote: the type of G(base) is a proposition (as ℤ is a set), so the information for G(loop) is redundant
note: This is a general principle: circle induction into a family of propositions needs only the base case.

quote: If we think of the circle as unit length complex numbers, then f_x(y) corresponds to the usual product xy
note: This footnote is an analogy with complex multiplication and rotations. It is outside the type-theoretic setting.

quote: combining the above two exercises yields an equivalence from (S¹ = S¹) to (S¹ ⊔ S¹)
note: This is the unnumbered conclusion after xca:(S1->S1)_(f)-eqv-S1. That inventory entry notes it.

quote: By cor:univ-covers-S1, exp and its friends uc_base : S¹ → Set and cst_base : 1 → S¹ are appearances of the universal covering
note: The generic lemma for pointed groupoids, together with circle_groupoid, covers cst_base. The formalization does not instantiate it separately.

quote: the circle is equivalent to the connected component of (ℤ,s) in the type Σ_{X:U}(X → X)
note: This is a forward statement of thm:S1bysymmetries.

quote: infinite cycles: sets X with a successor function t such that (X,t) can be merely identified with (ℤ,s)
note: This is a footnote. The formalization shows that elements of the component carry the cycle structure.

quote: When restricting to corresponding connected components, we get equivalences between these.
note: This is the generic restriction of equivalences to components, applied to coverings of the circle.

quote: components of Σ_{X:Set}(X ≃ X), which correspond to components of Σ_{X:U}(X → X) at pairs (X,t), where X is a set with a permutation t
note: Let X be a set with a permutation t. Module 288 proves that the component of ((X,_),t) in Σ_{X:Set}(X ≃ X) is equivalent to the component of (X,t) in Σ_{X:U}(X → X). The equivalence forgets the structure. The same is true for the component of a covering and its monodromy.

quote: for any (Y,u) in the same connected component of Σ_{X:U}(X → X) as (X,t), Y also is a set and u also a permutation
note: Module 288 proves that the property of being a set with an equivalence is a proposition on Σ_{X:U}(X → X). Thus every (Y,u) in the component of a set with a permutation is again a set with a permutation.

quote: we have an equivalence between the identity type (X,t) = (Y,u) and the sum type Σ_{e:X≃Y} et = ue
note: Module 288 proves (X,t) = (Y,u) in Σ_{X:U}(X → X) ≃ Σ_{e : X ≃ Y}(e∘t = u∘e) for arbitrary types. The equivalence uses the book's map: the transport equivalence of the type path, and the image of the path over it.

quote: These types are sets whenever X and Y are, and then we may write et = ue.
note: Module 288 proves that these types are sets when Y is a set. The book assumes that X and Y are sets. Then et = ue is a proposition.

quote: given a set X with a permutation t, we have an equivalence from (ℤ,s) = (X,t) to Σ_{e:ℤ≃X} es = te
note: This is a special case of the path characterization for sets with permutations.

quote: any power s^n of s itself gives a symmetry (s^n,p) : (ℤ,s) = (ℤ,s), where p is a proof of s^n s = s s^n
note: The commutation type is a proposition (rem:bang). Every power gives a loop.

quote: In particular, ev_0 : ((ℤ,s) = (ℤ,s)) → ℤ is an equivalence, mapping s^n to n for all n : ℤ.
note: The proof of thm:S1bysymmetries uses this.

quote: we often leave out the propositional data pertaining to InfCyc (and other subtypes) from the notation
note: This is a notational convention. The project always carries the propositional components.

quote: ev_U maps uc_base to (base = base, loop·–), identified with (ℤ,s); hence ev_U restricts to an equivalence between the components
note: Module 288 shows that ev_U(uc_base) is literally (base = base, p ↦ p·loop). It identifies this with (ℤ,s) through n ↦ loopⁿ. Also, ev_U restricts to an equivalence from the component of uc_base in S¹ → U onto InfCyc.

quote: The equivalence preim maps cst_base to (x:S¹) ↦ Σ_{_:1}(x = base) which can be identified with uc_base
note: Module 288 identifies preim(1, cst_z) = (x ↦ Σ_{_:1}(x = z)) with uc_z as a family, for every z.

quote: Both the left and the right triangle represent identity types ... we apply circle induction to construct an element of ∏_z c(z) = ev_U(uc_z)
note: Module 288 proves both triangles of eq:setbundle-Sc-univ-comp: preim ∘ (1, cst_–) = uc_– and ev_U ∘ uc_– = c. It uses the book's element of ∏_z c(z) = ev_U(uc_z). The right triangle compares the two pointed maps by their loops (both have coordinate −1). It uses the pointed universal property, not a literal circle induction.

quote: Another option would have been ... sending n to loop^{−n} ... You can move the minus sign around, but it has to pop up somewhere.
note: This is a footnote on orientation conventions. It has no mathematical claim beyond def:S1toC.

quote: we see that c is an equivalence if and only if either of the two other downward maps are
note: Module 288 proves BookIsEquiv c ≃ BookIsEquiv uc_– ≃ BookIsEquiv (1, cst_–). The proof uses 2-out-of-3 on the triangles.

quote: At this point we could conclude with an appeal to xca:TTYoneda, yielding that uc_– is an equivalence.
note: This is a footnote. The formalization proves it for every connected type.

quote: We now show that the map (1, cst_–) on the left is an equivalence ... Σ_{z:S¹}(base = z) is indeed contractible
note: Module 288 shows that the fiber of (1, cst_–) over (1, cst_base) is Σ_{z:S¹}(base = z). This fiber is contractible, so (1, cst_–) is an equivalence onto its component. With the triangles, this assembles the book's first proof that c is an equivalence.

quote: f is a covering over S¹ if and only if each map induced by f on identity types is injective
note: This is the Chapter-2 cor:fib-vs-path(set-fib-vs-path) for an arbitrary codomain.

quote: By xca:covering-utils(cover-n-type) A is a groupoid.
note: This is a margin note.

quote: the condition that each ap_f is injective can be relaxed to ap_f : (a₀ = a₀) → (f(a₀) = f(a₀)) being injective
note: This is the Chapter-2 cor:fib-vs-path(set-fib-vs-path-point) for connected A.

quote: Since A is connected, the proposition g_f⁻¹(n) does not depend on the choice of a₀, so the subset only depends on f
note: This is a margin note. The images at every point are equal to H_t.

quote: Such subsets of ℤ are closed under addition and negation ... since ap_f, wdg and loop^– are compatible with these operations
note: The proof uses the identification of the image with H_t (lem:cycle-order-point-ap) and the closure of H_t.

quote: The relation ∼ is an equivalence relation. (Exercise: Check this.)
note: This is an embedded exercise inside def:connected-by-t.

quote: It's easy to check that g and h are mutually inverse.
note: This is a left-to-the-reader step of con:cycset-connS1cover.

quote: the set {1,2,3,4,5} with the permutation 1↦2↦3↦1, 4↦5↦4. There are two components
note: This is a concrete example (fig:two-comp-S1-cover). It follows from con:cycset-connS1cover, but the formalization does not compute it.

quote: Our cycles are a special case of what is elsewhere called cyclically ordered sets ... closely related to the cyclic sets of Connes
note: This is a footnote about external notions.

quote: the universal covering ... equal to the exponential covering, which in turn corresponds to the infinite cycle (ℤ,s) ... Another example is the left one
note: The formalization proves that both examples are connected coverings with the stated cycles.

quote: Eventually we'll show -- assuming a weak form of LEM -- that these (with the universal covering) are all the decidable connected coverings
note: This is a forward reference to lem:componentsofcoversofS1.

quote: On loops, the degree m function is (–)^m, which is indeed an injection for positive m, so dg_m is a covering
note: This includes the subset {loop^{mn}} as the winding image mℤ.

quote: As a subset of ℤ, this is simply all multiples of m.
note: This is a margin note.

note: This is the printed case formula on remainders, transported to Fin m.

quote: Thus, (Fin m, s) is another key example of a cycle called the standard finite m-element cycle.
note: The formalization proves the cyclicity of the standard finite cycle.

quote: To identify dg_m and pow_m as coverings over S¹, it suffices to define an equivalence ψ_m and an identification α_m
note: The formalization proves the resulting identification of coverings.

quote: a_k :≡ pair(loop, refl_{s(k)}) : (base,k) = (base,s(k)). The m-th power map sends each mark to base and each arc to loop.
note: The arcs use the path lifting of R_m along loop, not refl_{s(k)}.

quote: the type of coverings over the circle is a groupoid
note: This is an instance of lem:setbundle-is-groupoid.

quote: Recall that Sub(ℤ) ≡ (ℤ → Prop) is a set.

note: This is a left-to-the-reader step in the proof of lem:IdCycle.

quote: By H ⊆ ℤ being closed under addition and negation, we simply mean that if z,z′ are in H, then so are z+z′ and −z.
note: This is a footnote of cor:set-trunc-cyc.

note: The formalization proves the 'it is clear' step of cor:set-trunc-cyc.

quote: we should write SetBundle(S¹)_U, Cyc_U, Order_U, etc. ... We trust that the reader can fill these in
note: This is a margin note on universe levels. Narya has a single Type. Modules 190–193 model universes as predicates.

quote: We have a canonical injection N ↪ Order, mapping 0 to the infinite order and each positive n to the finite order n.

note: The standard cycle of any order is ℤ modulo the period subgroup. The formalization proves that its order is equal to d.

note: The formalization defines ∼_d from order_periods d (set-truncation elimination). Thus the independence of the representative is built in.

note: This is a metatheoretic non-constructivity claim. The formalization has no weak counterexample (principality ⇒ LPO).

quote: This rules out certain pathological cycles, such as ... (e^{2παi})^n ... where α is an unknown real number
note: This is a footnote example with the reals.

note: This is an independence result about models. It is not expressible inside the theory.

quote: the Limited Principle of Omniscience is not constructive ... we could simply decide ... Goldbach conjecture
note: This is a Brouwerian argument in a footnote.

quote: LPO makes it possible to prove that the canonical map N → Order^dec ... is an equivalence
note: LPO is an explicit hypothesis. The formalization assumes nothing classical globally.

quote: the map is an injection, and a cycle (X,t) has infinite order iff H_t = {0}, and finite order m iff H_t = mℤ
note: This follows from the injectivity of order_periods and the computation of principal period subgroups.

quote: a decidable subset, since t^n = id is a proposition, and n is in H iff t^n(x) = x for some/all x
note: Decidable equality of the carrier gives decidability of the period predicate. Fixed points at one point give periods.

quote: If P(n) is constant 0, then H = {0}, so (X,t) has infinite order. (As a covering, it is then equivalent to the universal covering.)
note: This includes the identification of the infinite-order covering with the universal covering.

quote: if n₀ is the smallest natural number with m :≡ n₀+1 in H, then we claim H = mℤ
note: The proof uses Euclidean division, as in the book.

note: This is a footnote of rem:flipthecircle.

quote: Since the starting point in a cycle doesn't matter, we could also have written, e.g., (3 1 2)(5 4).
note: Module 288 proves (a_1 a_2 … a_k) = (a_2 … a_k a_1) for pairwise distinct entries of a decidable set. It also proves the book's (1 2 3)(4 5) = (3 1 2)(5 4) on Fin 5 by computation.

quote: if a₁,…,a_k are pairwise distinct elements of a decidable set A, then we write (a₁ a₂ ⋯ a_k) for the permutation
note: This also covers k-cycle and transposition. The definition uses list lookup. The formalization proves the behaviour that defines it.

quote: if A is decidable, then we can decide whether an element is moved or is a fixed point
note: This is the remark after def:support-permutation.

quote: Thus, disjoint cycles commute, so when we express a permutation ... as a product of disjoint cycles, the order doesn't matter.
note: This is a footnote.

quote: To show this, first write the permutation as a composition of cyclic permutations, then apply xca:perm-prod-transpositions
note: Module 286 proves that every permutation of a finite set is an explicit composite of cyclic permutations (a_1 … a_k), k ≥ 2. There is one cyclic permutation per orbit. Each factor is then written as k−1 transpositions. This gives the corollary by the book's route.

quote: This representation is not unique, as for example (1 2) = (2 3)(1 3)(2 3) as permutations of {1,2,3}.
note: Module 288 proves (1 2) = (2 3)(1 3)(2 3) as self-equivalences of Fin 3 (rightmost factor first). The check is pointwise, by computation.

quote: we'll show that the parity (odd/even) of the number of transitions is invariant
note: This is a forward reference to cor:sign-defined in a later chapter, outside chapters 2–3.

quote: the bijection eq:type-factorial can be constructed for any decidable set. Escardó constructed ... for any type X ... Y′ is a subtype of Y
note: Module 288 proves Escardó's Aut(X+1) ≃ (X+1)′ × Aut(X) for every type X. The proof uses transpositions of isolated points. Local Hedberg (paths from an isolated point form propositions) makes Y′ a subtype of Y. The decidable-set case is permutation_option_equiv (module 175).

quote: Binomial coefficients are familiar from Pascal's triangle ... where each number is the sum of the two above, e.g. C(4,2) = 6.
note: The formalization defines binomial by Pascal's rule. It shows that binomial satisfies the factorial formula.

quote: The forgetful map from Cyc₀ to InfCyc is an equivalence. Therefore we consider Cyc₀ and InfCyc as definitionally equal.
note: This is a margin note. This explicit equivalence replaces the definitional identification.

quote: the universal covering over Cyc₀ is represented by the constant function cst_{pt₀} : 1 → Cyc₀
note: This is an instance of the generic universality lemma for pointed groupoids with constructed_circle_groupoid (Cyc₀ is a groupoid). The formalization does not state the instance separately.

quote: the fiber of this universal covering over (X,t) : Cyc₀ is (equivalent to) X itself
note: Module 288 proves that the fiber of cst_{pt₀} : 1 → Cyc₀ over (X,t) is equivalent to X. The equivalence sends (★, q) to the transport of 0 along q⁻¹ (lem:IdCisZet).

quote: only the loop^k where k is a multiple of k [sic: m] is in the image of dg_m
note: The formalization reads the printed 'multiple of k' as 'multiple of m'. It proves the corrected statement.

quote: iterating the m-th root we get an identification of type (ᵐ√t)^m(k,x) = (k,t(x)); hence the term m-th root is apt
note: This is used in lem:deg-m-on-Cyc and thm:fiber-cdg.

quote: Of course, it's also quite easy to write down an inverse of ᵐ√t given an inverse of t.
note: This is a margin note.

quote: the product of Fin m with an n-element set is an mn-element set
note: This is the generic cardinality of products of finite types.

quote: In terms of iterated addition, we have φ(k,r) = (z ↦ z+m)^r(k).
note: Module 288 proves that φ(k,r) = k + m·r is equal to the r-th power of translation by m at k. Here translation by m is int_translation_equiv, z ↦ m + z.

quote: the first projection of ap_{cdg_m}(e,!) is id × e : (Fin m × X) = (Fin m × X′)
note: The lem:deg-m-on-Cyc inventory entry notes this.

quote: (id × e)(k,x) = (k,e(x)) equals (ᵐ√e)^m(k,x) ... ap_{cdg_m}(t⁻¹,!) is indeed the m-th power of a generating loop
note: The formalization proves it with (ᵐ√t)⁻¹. The printed ᵐ√(t⁻¹) is not a symmetry of the root cycle.

quote: the composite c dg_m is given by ((ℤ,s),s^{−m}) and cdg_m c by ((Fin m × ℤ, ᵐ√s), id × s⁻¹)
note: This is the unpointed correspondence of dg_m and cdg_m under c. It includes 'transport of id × s⁻¹ along φ is s^{−m}'.

quote: the inverse of φ maps z : ℤ to the remainder and the integer quotient of z under Euclidean division by m
note: This is a footnote.

note: This is the composite of the fiber equivalence with Fin m ≃ X/m. The formalization defines X/m as printed.

quote: (Such an r is unique if it exists.)
note: Module 288 proves that for an infinite cycle, the witness r with x′ = t^{mr}(x) is unique (ModWitness is a proposition).

quote: Then (Y,t^m) is an infinite cycle and we can construct a natural identification i : (X,t) = (Fin m × Y, ᵐ√(t^m))
note: For an infinite cycle, module 288 shows that the sketched map Y ↦ (Y, t^m, i) : X/m → cdg_m⁻¹(X,t) is h(P, –). Here e(k,x) = t^k(x) gives the identification i. The map is an equivalence into the fiber over Cycles. It is also an equivalence into the book's fiber Σ_{(Y,u):Cyc₀}((X,t) = cdg_m(Y,u)) of cdg_m : Cyc₀ → Cyc₀.

quote: The map defined by e(k,x) :≡ t^k(x) is an equivalence from Fin m × Y to X such that te = e ᵐ√(t^m).
note: This is a footnote. It applies to infinite cycles.

quote: The reader will no doubt have noticed that X/m is a finite cycle.
note: This is the basis of thm:image-Z-to-Cm.

quote: By lem:IdCycle, a necessary condition ... is H_t = H_{ᵐ√u} ... the fiber cdg_m⁻¹(X,t) is nonempty only if m divides the order of t
note: The formalization extracts the divisibility of the order from any identification with a root cycle.

quote: Here we take V not as a set, but as an element of the set X → Prop.
note: This is a margin note. Quotients are images in predicates (module 41).

quote: When X is a decidable set then LPO allows for a simpler formulation: P is either false ... or true, ... the preimage is X/m
note: Module 288 assumes LPO (LimitedOmniscience) as an explicit hypothesis and that X is a decidable set. Under these hypotheses, P is decidable. If ¬P, the fiber of cdg_m is empty. If P, the class map (Y,u,e) ↦ V_e is an equivalence onto X/m.

quote: Note that this doesn't depend on y, so that thm:wconstant-elim applies: (0,y) and (0,y′) are a distance mr apart
note: Module 288 proves that V_e is the class [e⁻¹(0,y)] for every y : Y. Here V_e is the subset fst(e(x)) = 0 (module 140). Hence V_e is independent of y. The proof uses membership in V_e, not thm:wconstant-elim.

quote: As a subset of X, V_e = {x : X | fst(e(x)) = 0}.
note: The formalization characterizes membership in V_e by the condition that the first coordinate of e is 0.

quote: to define the function h : P × X/m → cdg_m⁻¹(X,t), fix an equivalence class V of X/m, and assume that m divides the order
note: Module 288 gives the book's h : P × X/m → cdg_m⁻¹(X,t), (pr, V) ↦ ((V, t^m), i), for every cycle. Here i is the identification (X,t) = (Fin m × V, ᵐ√(t^m)) given by e′(k,v) = t^k(v).

quote: Then (V,t^m) is a cycle. Indeed t^m is properly restricted to V: if x lies in V, then so does t^m(x).
note: The formalization proves it for every cycle, not only for infinite cycles.

quote: e′ : Fin m × V → X, e′(k,v) :≡ t^k(v), which preserves cycle structure ... e′ is an equivalence if H_t ⊆ H_{ᵐ√(t^m)}
note: Module 288 proves that e′ is an equivalence whenever H_t ⊆ H_{ᵐ√(t^m)} (xca:map-of-cycles). P gives this inclusion for every cycle by the printed computation. Module 272 covers only infinite cycles.

quote: Straight from these definitions, we see that g∘h = id.
note: Module 288 proves g ∘ h = id for every cycle. The class of h(pr,V) is V because e′(0,v) = v.

quote: We leave to the reader to check that h∘g = id.
note: Module 288 proves h ∘ g = id directly. For (Y,u,e), the class V_e with t^m is isomorphic to (Y,u) by v ↦ snd(e(v)). The inverse is y ↦ e⁻¹(0,y). Also, e agrees with e′⁻¹ followed by this isomorphism. The reason is that both are maps of cycles that agree on V_e. With g ∘ h = id, this proves thm:fiber-cdg by the book's route (lem:weq-iso). This proof does not depend on module 140.

quote: to say something about the fact that each fiber of cdg_m carries a cycle structure
note: The fibers of cdg_m are identified with X/m. X/m carries the quotient cycle structure.

quote: Here p is surjective and i is injective, and any such factorization is equivalent to this one.
note: This recalls chapter-2 xca:unique-fact-image.

quote: for any surjection g and injection h with f = hg one can construct a (unique) equivalence e with g = ep, i = he
note: This is eqn:image-univ-prop. The uniqueness is of e with both triangles and their coherence with the square.

quote: Uniqueness of e above also follows from the following two exercises.
note: Module 288 shows that the uniqueness of e follows from xca:cancel-injection alone, through the triangle i = he. This holds for e as a map, and as an equivalence with both triangles. The printed xca:cancel-surjection is false (module 40). Its restriction to sets gives uniqueness from the other triangle when X is a set.

quote: Observe that im_{−1}(f) ≡ im(f).
note: This holds judgmentally.

quote: If A and B are sets ... im_0(f) amounts to the set of pairs (b,a) such that b = f(a)
note: Let A and B be sets. Module 288 proves that the fibers of f are sets. It also proves im₀(f) ≃ Σ_{b:B}Σ_{a:A}(b = f(a)), and this type is a set.

quote: Thus, any type is (−2)-connected, since its (−2)-truncation is contractible.
note: Module 285 states the (−2)-connectedness of types with the (−2)-truncation Unit. Every type is (−2)-connected.

quote: the (−1)-connected types are precisely the nonempty ones, and the 0-connected types are those we have called connected
note: Both comparisons are equivalences of propositions.

quote: One may verify now that the (−1)-connected functions are the surjections, and the (−1)-truncated functions are the injections.
note: (−1)-connected maps agree judgmentally with the earlier surjection notion. The formalization compares (−1)-truncated maps with embeddings.

quote: There is a factorization f = ip ... p(a) :≡ (f(a), |(a, refl)|_n), and i :≡ fst
note: This is eqn:n-image-factorization. The triangle holds by reflexivity.

quote: Every map f is trivially (−2)-connected. Moreover, fst : im_{−2}(f) → B is an equivalence and (−2)-truncated maps are precisely equivalences.
note: This is a margin note. The map fst is an equivalence because MinusTwoImage :≡ Σ B Unit.

quote: The map i is n-truncated, because ... the fiber i⁻¹(b) is equivalent to ||f⁻¹(b)||_n. Furthermore ... p is n-connected.
note: The inventory note of def:n-image states this.

quote: the fiber of p′ at any (b,t′) is equivalent to the fiber of |–|_n at t′
note: This is a footnote.

quote: Since P(b) is an n-type, we have the canonical equivalence ||Σ_{y:P(b)} Q(b,y)||_n → Σ_{y:P(b)} ||Q(b,y)||_n
note: This is a separate fact. The proof of thm:n-im-univ-prop uses it.

quote: we have a map –/m : Cyc₀ → Set, which we identify with the family R_m : S¹ → Set by precomposing with c
note: Module 288 proves –/m ∘ c = R_m in S¹ → Set for every CircleSignature. Here c : S¹ → Cyc₀ is the inverse of forgetting, composed with circle_infinite_cycle_map. The value c(loop) is the predecessor. Thus the pointed identification (ℤ/m, t̄⁻¹) = (Fin m, succ) with [0] ↦ 0 matches the monodromies.

quote: For every infinite cycle (X,t), the set X/m has m elements
note: Every infinite cycle has an order that is divisible by m. Thus Fin m ≃ X/m by lem:X-mod-m-chosen.

quote: the (−1)-image is readily identified with FinSet_m, the groupoid of m-element sets
note: Module 288 proves that each X/m for (X,t) : Cyc₀ is merely Fin m. It also proves that the (−1)-image of –/m is equivalent, over Set, to the book's FinSet_m = Set_(Fin m).

quote: To see that e is well defined ... Also, e preserves cycle structure.
note: This is a footnote in the proof of thm:image-Z-to-Cm.

quote: The theorem and its proof in fact generalize to cycles of all orders.
note: This is the content of xca:image-Cmd-to-Cm.

quote: This point has a symmetry σ_n :≡ (s⁻¹,!) ... all symmetries of pt_n are of the form σ_n^i for i = 0,…,n−1
note: σ_n is the predecessor symmetry. Remainder n enumerates the loops at pt_n.

quote: Proofs of the equation refl = σ_n^n ... are mapped by ap_f to proofs of refl = ap_f(σ_n)^n. Hence ... ev_{n,A} is well defined
note: The formalization proves refl = σ_n^n in pt_n = pt_n. It defines ev_{n,A} on this basis.

quote: The construction of f is really a special case of the delooping of the abstract group homomorphism σ_n^i ↦ σ^i
note: This is a margin note that points to sec:delooping (later chapter).

quote: for any G-set X, the type of fixed points of X is equivalent to the type of sections of Σ_{z:BG} X(z) → BG
note: This is a wip margin note. It is group-theoretic and not formalized.

quote: the corresponding families S : Cyc_n → Set are precisely those cycles (X,t) with t^n = id, i.e., whose order divides n
note: This is the corollary after prop:ump-cycn-into-groupoids.

quote: If we restrict to decidable connected coverings, equivalently, decidable cycles, these are the usual finite cycles with order dividing n.
note: Module 285 proves that decidable connected coverings over Cyc_n are the decidable cycles with tⁿ = id. These are the finite cycles (ℤ/(m+1), s) where m+1 divides n.

quote: an order p divides an order q iff there is a map of cycles from a cycle of order q to one of order p
note: This is a wip section.

quote: subgroups of C_n: C_k where k | n, connected set bundles of Cyc_n
note: This is a wip outline. The covering part is formalized (cyc_connected_set_families). The subgroup statement is not formalized.

quote: Bijective proof of mn = lcm(m,n) × gcd(m,n) via the product of cycles. Chinese remainder stuff.
note: The identity is not formalized (gcd/lcm exist in module 148).

quote: the identity type $a\eqto_Aa$ reflects the ``symmetries'' of an element $a$ in a type $A$.
note: Motivation for the view of loops as symmetries.

quote: Since the symmetries $p : a\eqto_A a$ are paths that start and end at the point $a:A$, we also call them \emph{loops} at $a$, or \emph{automorphisms} of $a$.
note: Terminology. The type of loops at the point of a pointed type is Loop (module 00), pointed as Omega.

quote: Symmetries have special properties.  For instance, you can rotate a square by $90\mathdegree$, and you can reverse that motion by rotating it by $-90\mathdegree$.
note: Geometric illustration.

quote: Symmetries can also be composed, and this composition respects certain rules that hold in all examples.
note: The composition of symmetries is usym_mul. Its laws are lem:idtypesgiveabstractgroups (usym_abstract_laws, module 403).

quote: it became clear to mathematicians at the end of the 19\textsuperscript{th} century that the properties of such symmetries could be codified by saying that they form an abstract \emph{group}.
note: Historical remark.

quote: equality is ``reflexive, symmetric and transitive'' -- implemented by operations $\refl{a}$, $\symm_{a,b}$ and $\trans_{a,b,c}$, and an abstract group is just a set with such operations satisfying appropriate rules.
note: The term refl is native. The operations symm and trans are inverse and concat (J.ny, module 00). Abstract groups are AbstractGroup (module 403).

quote: The axioms for an abstract group follow from the rules for identity types, without us needing to impose them.
note: lem:idtypesgiveabstractgroups: usym_abstract_laws and abstr (module 403).

quote: We will show in~\cref{ch:absgroup} that the two approaches give the same end result.
note: Forward reference to chapter 7 (groups compared with abstract groups). It is not part of this chapter.

quote: ``homomorphisms'' (which to us are simply given by pointed maps)
note: GroupHom G H is a wrapped BookPointedMap (BG G) (BG H) (module 401).

quote: In most of our exposition we make the blanket assumption that the identity type in question is a set, but in~\cref{sec:inftygps} we briefly discuss $\infty$-groups, where this assumption is dropped.
note: Groups require a groupoid classifying type. Thus USym G is a set. The type of ∞-groups (no groupoid condition) is InftyGroup (module 485).

quote: In order to motivate the formal definition of a group we revisit some types that we have seen in earlier chapters, paying special attention to the symmetries in these types.
note: Section introduction.

quote: Note that the types $\Sc$ and $\FinSet_2$ in the examples above are groupoids.
note: The lemma circle_groupoid holds for every circle. FinSet_2 is BΣ_2, a groupoid (bg_groupoid (symmetric_group two)).

quote: For an arbitrary type $A$ and an element $a:A$, the symmetries of $a$ in $A$ form an \inftygp, cf.~\cref{sec:inftygps} below.
note: Module 485 gives Aut_A(a) as an ∞-group for every A and a.

quote: in elementary texts it is customary to restrict the notion of a group to the case when $a\eqto_A a$ is a \emph{set}, as we will do
note: Group is defined from pointed connected groupoids.

quote: if are we given two elements $g,h:a\eqto_A a$, then the identity type $g\eqto h$ is a proposition (and we can simply write $g = h$). That is, $g$ can be equal to $h$ in at most one way
note: By the definition of isSet, usym_set G g h : isProp (g = h).

quote: The examples of groups that Klein and Lie were interested in often had more structure on the set $a\eqto_A a$, for instance a topology or a smooth structure.
note: Historical remark on topological and Lie groups.

quote: Such groups give rise to \inftygps by converting continuous (or smooth) symmetries of $a$ in $A$ parametrized by the continuous (or smooth) real interval, into identifications
note: The text refers to cohesive/real-cohesive type theory (ft:cohesive). This development has no real numbers and no cohesion.

quote: See \cref{ch:grouphistory} for a brief summary of the history of groups.
note: Cross-reference.

quote: We are now ready to define the type of groups.
note: Transition sentence.

quote: Frequently we want to consider the symmetries $\loops(A,a)$ of some element $a$ in some groupoid $A$, so we introduce the following definition.
note: Motivation for def:automorphism-group.

quote: Some groups have the property that the order you compose the symmetries is immaterial.  The prime example is the group of integers $\ZZ\jdeq\mkgroup(\Sc,\base)$.
note: Z = circle_group C is abelian for every circle C (circle_loops_commute).

quote: Any symmetry is of the form $\Sloop^n$ for some integer $n$, and if $\Sloop^m$ is also a symmetry, then $\Sloop^n\Sloop^m=\Sloop^{n+m}=\Sloop^{m+n}=\Sloop^m\Sloop^n$.
note: Every symmetry is loop^{wind(g)} (circle_every_symmetry_power). In the book's order, loopⁿ · loopᵐ = loop^{n+m} (circle_power_mul). Also, n + m = m + n (int_add_comm).

quote: Such cases are important enough to have their own name:
note: Transition to def:abgp.

quote: We can visualize symmetries $g$ and $h$ commuting with each other in a group $A \jdeq\mkgroup(A,a)$ by the picture in the margin; going from (upper left hand corner) $a$ to (lower right hand corner) $a$ by either composition gives the same result.
note: Picture of the commutation square. Its content is IsAbelian (def:abgp).

quote: We'll see more examples of groups in~\cref{sec:sign-homomorphism,sec:bicycles} and indeed throughout the rest of the book.
note: Forward reference.

quote: Studying the identity type leads one to the definition of what an abstract group should be. We fix a type $A$ and an element $a:A$ for the rest of the section, and we focus on the identity type $a\eqto a$.
note: Motivation and a variable convention for the whole section.

quote: There is an element $\refl a : a \eqto a$. (See page \pageref{rules-for-equality}, rule \ref{E2}.) We set $e \defeq \refl a$ as notation for the time being.
note: The unit of loop_space_abstract_group A a h is refl a.

quote: For $g : a \eqto a$, the inverse $g^{-1} : a \eqto a$ was defined in \cref{def:eq-symm}. Because it was defined by path induction, this inverse operation satisfies $e^{-1} \jdeq e$.
note: In Narya's HOTT, inverse is defined by transport. The equation inverse(refl a) = refl a holds only as the identification inverse_refl (no regularity), not judgmentally. Checked: `refl` does not typecheck for this rule in the pinned Narya. The transport along a degenerate identity type stays stuck as .trr. Thus the judgmental part cannot be formalized. Only the identification can be formalized. Remains partly.

quote: For $g, h : a \eqto a$, the product $h \cdot g : a \eqto a$ was defined in \cref{def:eq-trans}. Because it was defined by path induction, this product operation satisfies $e \cdot g \jdeq g$.
note: h·g = trans(g)(h) is concat g h (loop_space_mul A a h g). The equation e·g = concat g refl = g holds only as the identification concat_p1, not judgmentally. Checked: `refl` does not typecheck for this rule in the pinned Narya. The transport along a degenerate identity type stays stuck as .trr. Thus the judgmental part cannot be formalized. Only the identification can be formalized. Remains partly.

quote: For any elements $g,g_1,g_2,g_3:a\eqto a$, we consider the following four identity types: the right unit law: $g \eqto g\cdot e$, the left unit law: $g \eqto e\cdot g$, the associativity law: $g_1\cdot(g_2\cdot g_3) \eqto (g_1\cdot g_2)\cdot g_3$, the law of inverses: $g\cdot \inv g \eqto e$.
note: The four laws are the fields unit_right, unit_left, assoc and inv_right of AbstractGroupLaws. The equations have the orientation of def:abstractgroup.

quote: In \cref{xca:path-groupoid-laws}, the reader has constructed explicit elements of these identity types.
note: The lemma loop_space_group_laws gives the four elements for every loop space a = a that is a set.

quote: If $a\eqto a$ is a set, then the identity types above are all propositions. Then, in line with the convention adopted in \cref{sec:props-sets-grpds}, we could simply say that \cref{xca:path-groupoid-laws} establishes that the equations hold.

quote: The two equivalence classes of directions of the complete graph on a $3$-element set.

quote: We get this $2$-element set as a quotient of the set of all possible ways of choosing an element from each $2$-element subset of $A$, where two different such choices are deemed the same if they differ in an \emph{even} number of pairs.
note: For n ≥ 2, Bsgn(A) is identified with the set of sign orderings of A (bsgn_quotient_path).

quote: Since choosing an element from a $2$-element set is equivalent to ordering it (\eg chosen element first),
note: A two-element type T is equivalent to the type of enumerations Fin 2 ≃ T. The equivalence takes the value at 0, so the chosen element comes first.
