quote: To see that this really defines an equivalence relation, it helps to generalize a bit. Thus, fix a finite set $E$, and let $P : E \to \BSG_2$ be a family of $2$-element sets with parameter type $E$.
note: All of lem:parityequiv is stated for a finite E (with IsFinite witness) and P : E → BookFiniteSetsAt 2.

quote: This makes sense because any $2$-element set is decidable, and a subset of a finite set specified by a decidable predicate is itself a finite set.
note: Footnote of the definition at group.tex:1473.

quote: We may apply the usual set-theoretic operators, such as union and set difference, to these subsets.
note: Not necessary: the proof of transitivity uses the parity cocycle (finite_true_count_xor) instead of unions and differences of subsets.

quote: Note also that the parity relation is itself decidable.
The $\sim$ relation is clearly symmetric, and it is reflexive, since the empty set has an even number of elements.
note: Proof of lem:parityequiv.

quote: To show transitivity, let $f_1,f_2,f_3:\prod_{e:E}P(e)$. We can partition $E$ according to whether the $f_i$ agree or disagree
note: Module 463 formalizes the book's argument, with subsets as Boolean predicates and Card as finite_true_count. It proves E12 ∪ E23 ∪ E13 = E (parity_venn_cover). It proves F_ij = E'_ik ⊔ E'_jk as a count (parity_venn_split, E'_ab = parity_venn_part). It proves Card(F12)+Card(F13)+Card(F23) = 2(Card(E'12)+Card(E'13)+Card(E'23)) (parity_venn_count). It also proves the consequences: transitivity (parity_venn_transitive) and that at least one F_ij is even (parity_venn_one_even). Module 451 also proves transitivity by the xor cocycle parity(f,h) = parity(f,g) xor parity(g,h).

quote: We also see that at least one of the $F_{ij}$'s has even cardinality, so the quotient has at most $2$ elements.
note: Of any three sections, two are related.

quote: Clearly, if $E$ is empty, then $\prod_{e:E}P(e)$ is contractible, so the quotient is contractible.

we may assume that $E$ is the $n$-element set $\set{1,\dots,n}$ (since $n>0$), and (by induction on $n$) that each set $P(e)$ is $\set{\pm 1}$ … Then any function is equivalent to either the all $+1$-function or the function that is $-1$ at $1$ and $+1$ otherwise
note: Proved without a reduction of E and P. For any base section f0 and point e0, every section is related to f0 or to f0 flipped at e0. The two classes are distinct. Finite choice gives f0 merely.

quote: Recall from~\cref{ex:bigproductofgroups} that we can form the product of any (finite) family of groups. In particular, if we take the constant family at $G$, indexed by a finite set $S$, we get a power $G^S$, with classifying type $\BG^S$ and underlying set of symmetries $\USymG^S$.
note: Core module 407 (power_group S hS G, with USym ≃ S → USym G through happly).

note: Footnote of the exercise at group.tex:1570.

quote: This term is used in analogy with total and cyclic orderings, even though it's harder to visualize as an ordering. It seems to have first been used by~\citeauthor{Kuperberg1996}.
note: Terminological and historical footnote.

note: Forward reference to kernels (chapter 9). Here, the formalization proves only USym A_n ≃ even permutations (alternating_usym_even).

quote: Something interesting happens when we consider permutations on other shapes in $\BSG_n$, \ie arbitrary $n$-element sets $A$. The same map, $\Bsgn$, can be considered as a map $\BAut(A) \to \BSG_2$, but we can cannot make this pointed uniformly in $A$.
note: For n ≥ 2, there is no family of identifications Bsgn(A) = sh_{Σ_2} (bsgn_no_uniform_pointing).

quote: Why not? A construction $p : \prod_{A:\BSG_n}(\Bsgn_\div(A) \eqto \sh_{\SG_2})$ would amount to an identification of $\Bsgn$ with the constant map.
note: The equivalence with identifications Bsgn = const is function extensionality. For n ≥ 2, such an identification does not exist, because the transposition (0 1) is sent to the swap.

quote: However, the self-identifications of a $2$-element set $T$, $(T \eqto T)$, \emph{can} be identified with $\set{\pm1}$, according to whether it transposes the elements of $T$, or not.
note: For every point T of BΣ_2.

quote: In this section, we identify $\USG_2$ with the set $\set{\pm1}$, which has a compatible abstract group structure given by multiplication.
note: USym Σ_2 ≃ {±1} as abstract groups.

quote: Hence, we can define the sign of any permutation of a finite set:
For permutations of the standard $n$-element set, this is the same as the value $\Usgn(\sigma) : \USG_2$.
note: For n ≥ 2. For n ≤ 1, both are trivial.

quote: Note that $\sgn$ defines an abstract homomorphism from $\Aut(A)$ to $\SG_2$ for each $A$, since it does so for $A \jdeq \sh_{\SG_n}$.
note: Multiplicativity is proved directly for every point A, because loops of composites are concatenations. Transport invariance relates arbitrary A to the standard shape.

quote: Even better, this abstract homomorphism comes from a concrete one $\sgn^A : \Hom(\Aut(A),\SG_2)$ for each finite set $A$. Indeed, since $T \eqto U$ is a $2$-element set for any $2$-element sets $T$ and $U$, we can consider the map $\Bsgn^A_\div : \BAut(A) \to \BSG_2$ that maps $B : \BAut(A)$ to $(\Bsgn_\div(A) \eqto \Bsgn_\div(B))$.
note: sgn^A is constructed for a point A0 of BΣ_n. Here Aut(A0) = permutation_group, and Bsgn^A(B) = (Bsgn(A0) = Bsgn(B)) as a two-element set. Module 462 proves that sgn^A induces the sign of permutations. The statement is sigma_two_sign (USym sgn^A (g)) = sgn of the permutation of g (sign_aut_usym_sign). That is, USym sgn^A (σ) = sgn(σ) for every permutation σ of a finite set A (sign_aut_usym_permutation_sign_finite). Key step: transport in Bsgn^A along a loop is postcomposition. It moves iff the loop of Bsgn(A) moves.

quote: The identification of $\Bsgn^A_\div(A)$ with $\{\pm1\}$ mentioned above makes $\Bsgn^A_\div$ into a pointed map $\Bsgn^A : \BAut(A) \ptdto \BSG_2$, i.e., it defines an homomorphism $\sgn^A : \Hom(\Aut(A),\SG_2)$, as announced.
note: Pointing through Fin 2 ≃ {±1} ≃ (T = T).

quote: This is an instance of a more general construction, called {\em delooping} (see \cref{sec:delooping}). The formula for $\Bsgn^A_\div$ here is very simple since $\SG_2$ is a fairly simple group.
note: Forward reference.

quote: For \ref{it:sign-transposition}, it suffices to consider the transposition $(1\;2)$ of a standard $n$-element set $\set{1,2,\dots,n}$. Relative to the standard local ordering ($1<2,1<3,\dots,1<n,2<3,\ldots,n-1<n$), the transposition only changes the ordering $1<2$ to $2<1$, thus differing at exactly one place.
note: Reduction by transport invariance and conjugation. Inversions count the disagreement with the standard local ordering, and (0 1) has exactly one inversion.

quote: Now \ref{it:sign-cycle} follows via~\cref{xca:perm-prod-transpositions}.
For \ref{it:identity-even}, assume $\id_A = (a_1\;b_1)\cdots(a_k\;b_k)$, and take the sign of both sides. Since $\sgn$ is a homomorphism, we get $+1 = (-1)^k$, so $k$ is even.
(or of any totally ordered $n$-element set -- but these are all uniquely identified with $\bn n$)
note: This development does not include total orders on n-element sets. The exercise is formalized for Fin n with its standard order.

quote: If we represent $\sigma$ graphically as in~\cref{fig:permutation-crossings}, then inversions are crossings of the edges $(i,\sigma(i))$ and $(j,\sigma(j))$.
note: Pictorial interpretation of inversions.

These gave rise to the group of integers $\ZZ$ via the infinite cycle $(\zet,\zs)$ ... and the cyclic groups of finite order $\CG_m$ via the finite cycles $(\bn m,\zs)$
note: Recap of chapter 3 and ex:cyclicgroups: Cycles (module 58), cyclic_group 0 = Aut_Cyc(Z, succ) (≃ Z) and cyclic_group_fin n = Aut_Cyc(Fin (n+1), s) (module 404).

quote: \caption{The infinite dihedral bicycle.}
note: The TikZ code of fig:infinite-bicycle agrees with def:Dinfty-Q (x_n = inl n, y_n = inr n). It has red arrows x_n → x_{n+1} and y_{n+1} → y_n, and blue arrows x_n ↔ y_n.

note: Both pictured structures are connected in the sense of def:bicycle (explicit words from a base point). The sentence 'We call these bicycles ... for reasons that will become clear later' is naming.

note: Holds by refl in two forms. The first form is written out with a, b, a⁻¹, b⁻¹ (litmus for the composition order). The second form is a composite of the integer powers.

note: Transition sentence. The definitions are def:Dinfty-Q.

quote: If $(X,a,b)$ and $(X',a',b')$ are elements of $\sum_{X:\UU}(X\to X)\times(X\to X)$, then univalence ... gives an equivalence $\bigl( (X,a,b) \eqto (X',a',b') \bigr) \equivto \sum_{e:X\equivto X'}(ea \eqto a'e) \times (eb \eqto b'e)$
note: For arbitrary types and endomaps, with ea = a'e an identification of functions X → X'. The equivalence of the first component is transport along the path of types (univalence with transport_univalence_equiv).

quote: to a type whose three components we can visualize as: [diagram]
note: Commutative-diagram picture of the three components.

note: tⁿ(t x) = t(tⁿ x) for every cycle and integer n.

note: The two examples are formalized. The words 'many' and 'fewer than desired' are informal.

note: Read off the TikZ: Fin 4, a = (0 1 2 3), and b swaps 0 and 2 and fixes 1, 3. Its symmetries are equivalent to Bool (identity and a²).

quote: This tells us what's special about the infinite dihedral and the quaternion bicycles: they are \emph{normal}.
note: Explicit symmetries reach every element from a base point. For Z ⊔ Z, these are the translations/reflections σ±_k. For Fin 8, these are the 8 permutations that commute with a, b. Then xca:normal-bicycle-equiv applies.

quote: What follows is a special case of a more general story that resumes in~\cref{def:normal-action} (for actions) and will be the focus of~\cref{ch:subgroups} on normal subgroups.
note: Forward reference (footnote).

quote: In other words, a normal bicycle has the maximum possible amount of symmetry, in that any element is just like any other.
note: Formal content: for every bicycle and x, ev_x : Aut(B) → X is an embedding (bicycle_evaluation_injective). Thus X bounds the symmetries. Normal means that ev_x is also surjective. It is sufficient that ev_x is merely surjective at one point (normal_bicycle_from_point_surjective). That is, the maximum Aut(B) ≃ X is attained. Then a unique symmetry moves every element to every other element. This is 'any element is just like any other' (bicycle_symmetry_between, normal_bicycle_unique_symmetry).

quote: In other words, for a normal bicycle $(X,a,b)$ there is a unique symmetry (\ie permutation of $X$ commuting with $a$ and $b$) mapping any $x$ to $x'$ for any $x,x':X$.
note: BookIsContr (Σ (e : BicycleIsomorphisms B B) (x' = e(x))).

quote: It follows that $\cbid xx = \id_X$ and $\cbid{x'}{x''} \circ \cbid{x}{x'} = \cbid x{x''}$.
note: As identifications of symmetries: cbid x x = refl and concat (cbid x x') (cbid x' x'') = cbid x x'' (g ∘ f is concat f g). Also, inverse (cbid x x') = cbid x' x.

note: By refl: the inverse map of the equivalence (ev_x, normality) at x' is cbid x x'.

quote: In~\cref{sec:covS1} we used the subset $H_t \jdeq \setof{n:\zet}{t^n=\id}$ of $\zet$ to study a cycle $(X,t)$. There, we get the equal subsets $\setof{n:\zet}{t^n(x)=x}$ no matter which $x:X$ we pick.

note: H_x as an element of Sub((Z⊔Z)*). The claim is the exercise at group.tex 2142.

quote: the following lemma is a corollary of a \emph{type-theoretic Yoneda lemma}, and the proof is \cref{xca:TTYoneda}.

so that the action of $\pathsp{\blank}^H$ gives us a path $\pi : \princ H \jdeq\pathsp{\sh_H}^H \eqto \pathsp{\Bf(\sh_G)}^H$. Combining we get $\inv\eta\pi:\princ H \eqto f_!\,\princ G$.

if $f:\Hom(G,H)$ is such that $\USymf$ is surjective, then $f^*$ embeds the type of $H$-sets as some of the components of the type of $G$-sets.

note: Forward reference to chapter 9.

note: Bρ_G(z) = (gset_paths G z (shape G), !) in Set_(USym G). The pointing path has the first component refl. The second component, which is propositional, is adjusted.

Note that the induced map on symmetries is: $\USym\rho_G:\USym G \to (\USym G \eqto \USym G): g \mapsto (x \mapsto x\inv g)$
note: As a permutation: permutation_action of USym ρ_G(g) sends x to usym_mul x g⁻¹ = concat g⁻¹ x (typal).

note: The picked-out symmetries are those in the image of USym ρ_G (lem:E-preserves-symms), that is, right multiplications by g⁻¹. The second component of the shape is (sh_G, pointing path of ρ_G), not literally id (its first component is refl).

note: The action of P_G is left multiplication (principal_gset_act). So the permutations that left multiplication selects are the USym of the alternative classifying map z ↦ P_G(z). note: Section title (historical remark on the attribution of the lemma). No mathematical claim.

note: For (x_O, f_O): USym G ≃ Σ_{y : X_O(sh_G)} USym G_{y}. Here cor:lagrange-dep-sum gives the stabilizers in X_O, and burnside_orbit_stabilizer_bridge identifies them with the stabilizers in X. The book does this silently.

quote: As a first application of Burnside's Lemma, we note the following number-theoretic consequence, which falls out when we consider the analog of exa:prep-burnside for the case of C_p acting on base-n sequences of length p.
note: Fermat's Little Theorem follows from burnside_lemma applied to the action of C_p on Fin p → Fin n (fermat_gset).

note: The underlying set is Fin p → Fin n by definition (refl). fin_function_equiv: (Fin k → Fin n) ≃ Fin (n^k), so the cardinality is n^p.

note: xca:lagrange for the subgroup (X_[f], f) gives p = Card(X_[f]) × Card((C_p)_f). The underlying group of this subgroup is the stabilizer (rem:subgrp-is-stabsubgr), and the tuple is orbit_subgroup of module 508. fermat_stabilizer_dichotomy: Card((C_p)_f) is 1 or p.

quote: The latter happens when f is one of the n constant functions.
note: 'All of C_p' is expressed as 'every symmetry fixes f'. This holds iff f is constant (f(k) = f(0) for all k). The constant functions form a copy of Fin n. The converse direction uses the symmetry g with g_*(0) = k (cor:id-m-cycle).

quote: The set Fin p -> Fin n is finite, hence decidable, so there is no risk to make a case-by-base analysis.
note: Footnote: a non-constant f merely has k with f(k) ≠ f(0), by the decidability of equality in Fin n and finite quantifiers. The case analysis of the main proof is instead on Card(X_[f]) ∈ {1, p} (primality).

quote: select k such that f(k) neq f(0), and surely s^k . f neq f: then s^k is not in UC_p the only option is that (C_p)_f is trivial.
note: s^k is the symmetry g with g_*(0) = k (fermat_power_symmetry, cor:id-m-cycle). If f(k) ≠ f(0), then s^k·f ≠ f (fermat_power_symmetry_moves). The conclusion 'only refl fixes a non-constant f' is fermat_fixed_nonidentity_constant (contrapositive form).

quote: More rigorously, s^k is not in the image of USym i_f where i_f: (C_p)_f -> C_p is the monomorphism defining the stablizer.
note: Every symmetry in the image of USym(i_x) fixes x (stabilizer_image_fixes, general G-sets). Hence s^k with f(k) ≠ f(0) is not in the image of USym(i_f).

quote: In other words, X^g is all of X(Fin p, s) for g = refl_{(Fin p, s)}, and only the constant functions for anyof the other p-1 symmetries in UC_p.
note: X^refl ≃ X(sh) (any G-set). For g ≠ refl, X^g ≃ constant functions ≃ Fin n. There are p − 1 symmetries g ≠ refl (Without (USym C_p) refl ≃ Fin (p−1)).

quote: n^p + n(p-1) = Card(sum_{g:UC_p} X^g) = Card(X/C_p) x Card(C_p) = Card(X/C_p) x p, and so we conclude that p divides n^p-n.
note: For p = m+1: Card(Σ_g X^g) = n^p + n·m (fermat_fixed_points_count, by separation of refl). This equals Card(X/C_p) × p by burnside_lemma and Card(C_p) = p (fermat_burnside_equation). fermat_divides_from_count derives p | n^p ∸ n with n ≤ n^p.

quote: We have seen that many types carry a notion of morphism between its elements: ... In all those cases, we have notions of identity morphism and composition of morphisms.
note: Functions, identifications, pointed maps, fiberwise maps, group homomorphisms and maps of G-sets have identities and composition. The formalization packages them as the wild precategories TypeWild, PathWild X, PointedWild, FamilyWild X, GroupWild and GSetWild G. The last one is FamilySetWild BG, and its arrows are by refl the chapter-5 GSetHom. The \wip item on cycles is not part of the text.

quote: taking underlying symmetries in groups, USym : Group → Set, comes with ... USym : Hom(G,H) → (USym G → USym H) satisfying USym(id_G) = id_{USym G} and USym(ψ∘φ) = USym ψ ∘ USym φ
note: The claim is usym_hom (chapter 4) with usym_hom_id and usym_hom_compose. Together they form the functor usym_functor : GroupWild → SetWild (ex:USym-functor).

quote: prepare for the main result of the next chapter, ch:absgroup, which is to give an equivalence of categories between the categories of concrete and abstract groups
note: This is a forward reference to chapter 7. Chapter 7 proves the equivalence with GroupCat (module 686) and the equivalence criteria of this chapter (ff_eso_is_cat_equivalence, cat_equivalence_from_nat_isos).

quote: we have already seen some examples of adjunctions, for example in xca:adjunction-_!-^*, xca:adjunction-^*-_*
note: The bijections of xca:adjunction-_!-^* and xca:adjunction-^*-_* are the transpositions of the adjunctions f_! ⊣ f^* and f^* ⊣ f_* between GSetCat G and GSetCat H (module 690). These adjunctions are instances of the family-of-sets adjunctions of module 664.

quote: We have also seen an incarnation of the Yoneda lemma in xca:TTYoneda; in sec:yoneda we treat the O.G. version.
note: This is an analogy between the type-theoretic Yoneda lemma (module 95) and the categorical one (module 622). It is not a precise statement.

quote: We end with a brief introduction to monoidal categories in sec:monoidal-cats, as we'll see in ch:abelian that abelian groups form an example.
note: The section on monoidal categories is empty at the pinned commit. It has only LaTeX comments. The abelian-group example is a forward reference to chapter 12.

quote: As mentioned above, many types come equipped with notion of \emph{morphism} or \emph{arrow} between its elements which is more general than identification or \emph{isomorphism}. For instance we have type of functions $A \to B$ for $A,B:\UU$ and the type of pointed functions $A \ptdto B$ for $A,B:\UUp$. There are identity morphisms and composition of morphisms,
note: The claim is about identities and composition of functions and of pointed functions. The formalization organises them as the wild precategories TypeWild and PointedWild.

quote: However, when the types of morphisms $\hom(A,B)$ are \emph{sets}, then the types of $\lambda$, $\rho$, and $\alpha$ are propositions, so any coherence conditions are automatically fulfilled.
note: The families of λ, ρ and α are propositions when the hom types are sets. The coherences of rem:wild hold in every precategory. These coherences are λ = ρ at identities, the triangle and the pentagon.

quote: Most (wild) precategories we shall meet satisfy a further condition that makes them better behaved than arbitrary precategories: a \emph{univalence} condition.
note: This is the motivation for def:univalent-cat.

quote: In fact, for the wild precategory of types and functions, this condition is exactly the Univalence Axiom (\cref{def:univalence})!
note: For TypeWild, idtoiso followed by the comparison of isomorphisms with equivalences is ptoe (transport_equiv). Thus the univalence of TypeWild is equivalent to the statement that p ↦ ptoe(p) is an equivalence (2-out-of-3, module 151). The equivalence type is the native Equiv.

quote: The type $\isIso(f)$ is indeed a proposition,\footnote{This follows just as for functions: If $f$ is an isomorphism, then each factor in the product is contractible, as, e.g., $\sum_{g:B\to A}f\circ g\eqto\id_B$ is the fiber of $f\circ\blank : (B \to A) \to (B \to B)$ at $\id_B$, and all functions $f\circ\blank$ and $\blank\circ f$ are equivalences of types using the data that makes $f$ an isomorphism along with $\lambda$, $\rho$, and $\alpha$.}
note: This is the chapter-6 core (module 600). The proof follows the footnote exactly.

quote: and every identity arrow is an isomorphism. We write $\inv f$ for the inverse of an isomorphism $f$.
note: This is the chapter-6 core (module 600). The inverse of an isomorphism is cat_iso_inverse.

quote: Now we are ready to restate the examples mentioned in the introduction to the chapter. In each case we leave it to the reader to supply most of the data.
note: This text introduces the list of examples. The claims below supply the data.

quote: The \emph{wild category of types} (in universe $\UU$) has $\UU$ as its type of objects, and the function type $A \to B$ as its type of arrows for $A,B :\UU$. It is univalent by the Univalence Axiom.
note: This is the chapter-6 core (module 601). The universe is Narya's Type. TypeWildIn (module 606) is the version for a universe that a smallness predicate gives.

quote: The \emph{wild category of pointed types} (in a universe $\UU$) has $\UUp$ as its type of objects, and the type of pointed maps $A \ptdto B$ as its type of arrows.
note: The book calls it a wild category, so it is univalent. The formalization proves this. Isomorphisms of pointed types are the pointed maps whose underlying map is an equivalence. The type of pointed equivalences out of X is contractible (module 162).

quote: The \emph{wild category of families} over a given type $X$ has $X \to \UU$ as its type of objects, and the type of fiberwise maps $(X \to_B Y) \defeq \prod_{b:B}X(b) \to Y(b)$ as its type of arrows.
note: Module 604 defines FamilyWild, its univalence and FamilyWildCategory. Modules 662-664 use them again. Module 662 adds litmus checks: fiberwise negation is an iso, and it gives an identification of families. The book's formula mixes the names of the base and of the families.

quote: The \emph{category of sets} has $\Set$ as its type of objects, and the function type $A \to B$ as its type of arrows. It's a category since each type $A\to B$ is a set, and it's univalent.
note: This is the chapter-6 core (module 601).

quote: The category of groups has Group as its type of objects, and the homomorphism type (G → H) ≔ Hom(G,H) as its type of arrows.
note: The formalization gives GroupCat : Category. Its hom-sets come from lem:hom-is-set (group_hom_set). Its univalence comes from Id Group G H ≃ GroupIso G H (module 402) together with group_iso_cat_iso_equiv. The latter says that group isomorphisms are exactly the categorical isomorphisms.

quote: The category of G-sets, for a group G, has GSet as its type of objects, and the type of morphisms of G-sets Hom_G(X,Y) as its type of arrows.
note: GSetCat G : Category is FamilySetCategory (BG G .carrier). By refl, its objects are GSet G, its arrows are GSetHom G X Y and its composition is gset_hom_compose. It is univalent because (X = Y) ≃ ∏_z (X z ≃ Y z) ≃ (X ≅ Y) (family_set_univalent).

quote: Note that the category of sets sits inside the wild category of types.
note: SetWild is the full subcategory of TypeWild on the sets. The inclusion functor is fully faithful (full_subcat_inclusion, set_inclusion_fully_faithful: modules 620 and 627). It is also an injection on objects (module 618).

quote: By the univalence condition, in a category each identity type $A \eqto B$ is equivalent to the set $A \isoto B$, and is hence a set.
note: This is the chapter-6 core (module 600).

quote: And important special case is when each arrow type $A \to B$ is a \emph{proposition}.
note: This text introduces ex:poset.

quote: There's no conflict with the terminology introduced in~\cref{sec:props-sets-grpds}, because this construction gives an equivalence from the type of $1$-types (in $\UU$) to the type of groupoids (in $\UU$), as we shall see below in~\cref{thm:1types-are-groupoids}.
note: This is a forward reference. The equivalence is thm:1types-are-groupoids (modules 670–677). Here the book cites only the construction 1-type ↦ groupoid (path_groupoid_of_groupoid, core).

quote: \Cref{def:wild-cat,def:precategory,def:category,def:wild-pre-groupoid} are summarized as a diagram of inclusions in~\cref{fig:cat-summary}.
note: The inclusions of the cube are forgetful maps between the record types. They are projections of .wild and of the property fields. The named ones are core. The figure itself is a picture.

quote: Many notions in category theory work already at the level of wild categories, [...] but a notable exception is the construction of slice categories, (also known as \emph{over categories}).
note: We show that the slice of a wild precategory is a wild precategory when the pentagon and two unit-triangle coherences are given. We also show that slices of precategories always exist. The negative claim is that slices cannot be built for arbitrary wild precategories. This claim is a meta-statement and is not formalized.

quote: They \emph{all} work at the level of $(\infty,1)$-categories.
note: This text refers to (∞,1)-category theory (Lurie, Land). The book itself notes that the definition of (∞,1)-categories in this type theory is an open problem.

quote: Many concepts that we introduced in~\cref{ch:univalent-mathematics} for the wild category of types make sense in arbitrary wild precategories.
note: This text introduces section 6.3.

quote: The unit type $\bn 1$ is a terminal object in the wild category of types, and in the category of sets,
note: The clause on the trivial group in the category of groups is a separate record (trivial_group_terminal/trivial_group_initial, module 688).

quote: while the trivial group TG is a terminal object in the category groups.
note: The formalization proves IsTerminalObj (GroupCat .wild) trivial_group for the book's TG = Aut_Prop(true). Hom(G, TG) is contractible because B TG is a connected set, and thus contractible (module 431). The same holds for unit_group. GroupCat is univalent, so the type of terminal objects is contractible with the center TG. Thus TG = 1 as groups. Litmus tests: the unique Σ_3 → 1 is the homomorphism of ex:groups-morphisms (refl), and Σ_3 is not terminal. The sentence starts at line 452 with the claims about 1 in types and sets (module 607).

quote: The is a ``dual'' notion as well.
note: Initial objects of C are judgmentally the terminal objects of C^op.

quote: For example, the empty type $\bn 0$ is initial in the wild category of types,
note: The clause on the trivial group in the category of groups is a separate record (trivial_group_terminal/trivial_group_initial, module 688).

quote: while the trivial group TG is initial in the category of groups.
note: The formalization proves IsInitialObj (GroupCat .wild) trivial_group. Hom(TG, G) ≃ (B TG →* BG) is contractible because B TG is contractible (contractible_domain_pointed_maps, module 431). The same holds for unit_group, and TG is a zero object. The type of initial objects of GroupCat is contractible. Litmus test: Σ_3 is not initial, because Hom(Σ_3, Σ_3) has two different elements. The sentence starts at line 463 with the claim about 0 in types (module 607).

quote: The relationship between terminal and initial objects reflects a deep aspect of category theory: Every concept comes with a dual version obtained by ``reversing all the arrows''. More formally, can introduce for every wild precategory its opposite category that has its arrows reversed.
note: The general principle is not a single statement. The instances in this section (initial/terminal, epi/mono) hold judgmentally via OppositeWild.

quote: It follows that any construction or theorem about wild precategories has a dual version, obtained by precomposition with $(\blank)\op$.
note: This is a meta-principle. For example, the formalization uses it to get initial_objects_prop and initial_objects_iso as duals of the terminal versions.

quote: For example, the dual of the slice category construction is the \emph{coslice} category $C/\mathcal C$ (also known as the \emph{under category}).
note: The coslice c/C is defined as (C^op/c)^op via OppositeWild. The checks coslice_ob_unfold and coslice_hom_unfold show by refl that its objects are (A, f : c → A). They also show that its arrows are g : A → A' with g ∘ f = f'.

quote: As a further example of a pair dual notions, we consider that of monomorphisms and epimorphisms.
note: Epimorphisms of C are judgmentally the monomorphisms of C^op.

quote: If $C$ is a precategory, then these conditions reduce to the implications \[ f\circ g=f\circ h \to g=h, \quad\text{and}\quad g\circ f=h\circ f \to g=h, \] respectively.
note: Both directions are proved. For maps between sets, injectivity (propositional fibers) is equivalent to the reflection of paths.

quote: We already met the monomorphisms in the category of groups in def:typeofmono using a different definition.
note: The identification of the two notions is the content of the next exercise, xca:mono-cat-grp: IsMono (GroupCat .wild) H G i ≃ IsEmbedding (USym H) (USym G) (usym_hom H G i) (module 687).

quote: The epimorphisms in the wild category of types are always surjections,
note: The test object is Prop (PropTypes) with the predicates ∃-fiber and True, as for sets.

quote: but are much more restricted. See~\citeauthor{BdJR2025}\footcite{BdJR2025} for details.
note: An example shows this. The base point 1 → TwoSets is a surjection (module 40), but it is not an epimorphism of types (test object TwoSets). The characterization of the cited paper is not formalized.

quote: Not only do have arrows \emph{in} (wild pre-)categories, there's also a notion of arrow \emph{between} them. These are called functors.
note: This text introduces def:functor.

quote: In ch:absgroup we shall define the category of abstract groups, absGroup, in such a way that the map abstr : Group → absGroup from def:abstrG becomes a functor in line with the discussion from rem:first-abs-hom.
note: This is a forward reference to chapter 7, which defines the category of abstract groups. Chapter 7 will use the chapter-4 data abstr and abstr_hom (module 403). The corresponding functor to Set is usym_functor (module 686).

quote: There is in fact also a wild category of all wild precategories, but its notion of arrow is more refined than the wild functors of def:functor: We would need to include components corresponding to the unit and associativity laws as well.
note: The book does not define the refined notion of arrow, that is, wild functors with coherence components for the unit and associativity laws. We formalize only the plain version WildPrecatWild with wild functors. We show univalence after the restriction to precategories, where the law components are propositions.

quote: There's also a notion of arrow \emph{between functors}. These are called natural transformations.
note: Natural transformations are the arrows of the functor precategory: FunctorWild C D .hom F G ≡ WildNatTrans C (D .wild) F G.

quote: Freyd observed that ``categories are what one must define in order to define functors, and that functors are what one must define in order to define natural transformations.'' In this sense, natural transformations are at the heart of category theory.
note: This is a historical quotation in a footnote. It has no mathematical content.

quote: With natural transformations as arrows we can elevate the type of functors to a precategory.
note: FunctorPrecat C D (core module 602) is a precategory whose objects are the functors and whose arrows are natural transformations. Its hom-sets come from nat_trans_set.

quote: A functor $F : \mathcal C\op \to \mathcal D$ whose domain is an opposite category is called \emph{contravariant}, because it reverses the directions of arrows: $f : C \to_{\mathcal C} C'$ in $\mathcal C$ maps to $F(f) : F(C') \to_{\mathcal D} F(C)$ in $\mathcal D$.
note: A contravariant functor is a WildFunctor (OppositeWild C) D. The lemma contravariant_functor_action shows the reversed action f : c → c' ↦ F(f) : F(c') → F(c). This action is F .mor c' c f.

quote: If needed for emphasis, we may say that a functor $F : \mathcal C \to \mathcal D$ is \emph{covariant} by contrast.
note: This is terminology only. Covariant functors are plain WildFunctor C D.

quote: Given a group homomorphism f : G → H, there are families of bijections α : Hom_H(f_! X, Y) ≅ Hom_G(X, f^* Y), β : Hom_G(f^* Y, X) ≅ Hom_H(Y, f_* X) ... that are furthermore natural.
note: The maps α : Hom_H(f_! X, Y) ≃ Hom_G(X, f^* Y) and β : Hom_G(f^* Y, X) ≃ Hom_H(Y, f_* X) are transpositions. They belong to the wild adjunctions gset_induce_restrict_adjunction and gset_restrict_coinduce_adjunction (module 690). Naturality in both variables is part of RightAdjointData. The equivalences are gset_induce_restrict_transpose_equiv and gset_restrict_coinduce_transpose_equiv.

quote: This just means that if we fix either $X$ or $Y$, then we get natural transformations of the corresponding functors.
note: Naturality of a transposition means naturality in each variable separately. RightAdjointData has natural_left and natural_right. These are the squares of wild natural transformations for fixed d and for fixed c (adjunction_nat_trans_left/right). They are interchangeable with joint naturality on C^op × D (module 628). The surrounding G-set instance (f_! ⊣ f^* ⊣ f_*, lines 853-872) needs chapter 5 and is not formalized here.

quote: The essence of an adjunction is thus the ability to transpose between arrows $F(C) \to_{\mathcal D} D$ and $C \to_{\mathcal C} G(D)$.
note: The lemma adjunction_transposition gives the BookEquiv Hom_D(F c, d) ≃ Hom_C(c, G d) whose map is α_{c,d}.

quote: There is however another way of packaging this information. We can transpose the identity $\id_{F(C)}$ to get an arrow $\eta_C : C \to_{\mathcal C} GF(C)$, and the identity $\id_{G(D)}$ to get an arrow $\varepsilon_D : FG(D) \to_{\mathcal D} D$.
note: The unit is η_c = α(id_{F c}) and the counit is ε_d = α⁻¹(id_{G d}) (core module 603). Here α⁻¹ is the section that the isomorphism data supply. The lemma adjunction_counit_transpose gives α(ε_d) = id_{G d}.

quote: Naturality of $\alpha$ makes these into natural transformations $\eta : \id_{\mathcal C} \to GF$, and $\varepsilon : FG \to \id_{\mathcal D}$ called the \emph{unit} and \emph{counit} of the adjunction.
note: This is eq:adj-unit-counit. Every wild adjunction gives adjunction_unit_nat_trans : WildNatTrans C C (functor_identity C) (G ∘ F). It also gives adjunction_counit_nat_trans : WildNatTrans D D (F ∘ G) (functor_identity D). Their naturality comes from the naturality of α. The proof of the counit square uses the injectivity of α.

quote: Triangle laws for an adjunction $F \dashv G$: $\varepsilon_{F(C)} \circ F(\eta_C) = \id_{F(C)}$ and $G(\varepsilon_D) \circ \eta_{G(D)} = \id_{G(D)}$ (fig:adj-triangles).
note: The margin figure shows the two triangles (quoted here in formula form). They are proved for every wild adjunction in xca:adj-triangles.

quote: Conversely, given $F$, $G$, $\eta$, and $\varepsilon$, along with fillers for the triangle laws, we can recover $\alpha$ by sending $f : F(C) \to_{\mathcal D} D$ to the composite $C \xrightarrow{\eta_C} GF(C) \xrightarrow{G(f)} G(D)$.
note: The construction adjunction_from_triangles uses exactly α(f) = G(f) ∘ η_c. For an adjunction, adjunction_transpose_via_unit shows α(f) = G(f) ∘ η_c. Thus α is recovered from its own unit (adjunction_round_trip_transpose).

quote: We can thus go back and forth between the different bundles of data for a wild adjunction.
note: The formalization gives maps in both directions between RightAdjointData and UnitCounitAdjunction. The round trips return α, η and ε up to pointwise identifications, with the same G on the nose. An equivalence of the two types of bundles is not proved. It would need coherence of the wild identifications.

quote: We shall see later in~\cref{cor:adj-unique} for a functor whose domain is a category, that the data of a right adjoint is a proposition.
note: This is a forward reference to cor:adj-unique. The lemma right_adjoints_agree shows that any two right adjoints of F have identified right functors.

quote: One benefit of the Yoneda lemma is that we can characterize adjoint functors in terms of representability, and then derive the uniqueness of adjoint functors in the case of categories.
note: The lemma right_adjoint_data_representations_equiv gives RightAdjointData (C .wild) D F ≃ (d : D) → Σ x, Hom_D(F -, d) ≅ h_x (via lem:adj-via-repr). Uniqueness for categories is right_adjoint_data_prop.

quote: From cor:adj-unique we immediately see the following:
note: The formalization derives lem:cat-equiv-is-prop from cor:adj-unique (right_adjoint_data_prop, module 624). It also uses that the unit and counit isomorphism conditions are propositions. An independent proof is is_cat_equivalence_prop.

quote: It's often useful to show that a functor F : C → D is an equivalence by giving just a functor G : D → C along with natural isomorphisms η : id_C ≅ GF and ε : FG ≅ id_D. This is analogous to lem:weq-iso, and we refer to AKS2015 Lemma 6.2 for the implementation.
note: The proof is for wild precategories. The transposition is k ↦ G(k) ∘ η_c. G is fully faithful by 2-out-of-6. The unit G(id) ∘ η_c is a composite of isomorphisms. The counit is an isomorphism because G reflects isomorphisms. The right adjoint of the result is definitionally G itself.

quote: We again refer to AKS2015 Lemma 6.6 for details.
note: This is a bibliographic pointer. The lemma itself is fully formalized (cat_equivalence_ff_split_eso_equiv).

quote: From this we conclude that if C is category, then split essential surjectivity is equivalent to essential surjectivity, and then lem:equiv-precat-is-ff-split-eso gives one of the fundamental theorems of category theory
note: The lemma split_eso_eso_equiv says this: for a category C and a fully faithful F, IsSplitEso ≃ IsEso (BookEquiv). Together with lem:equiv-precat-is-ff-split-eso, this gives thm:ff-eso-equiv.

quote: Compare lem:inj+surj, stating that a function f : A → B of types is an equivalence if and only if it is injective and surjective.
note: This is a cross-reference to chapter 2. There, lem:inj+surj is embedding_surjection_equiv (module 12). The categorical analogue is the injectivity/image description of thm:ff-eso-equiv.

quote: There is also a version of this statement for precategories, but it concerns the stronger notion of isomorphism of precategories, i.e. fully faithful functors that induce an equivalence on the types of objects. The point is that for categories, this is the same as equivalence.
note: The lemma precategory_path_equiv says this: for precategories, the map (C = D) → PrecatIsomorphism C D is a BookEquiv. This map is defined by path induction (refl ↦ identity functor). The proof uses a structure identity principle. This principle contracts the object type, the hom family, the identities and the composition by univalence and function extensionality. The lemma precat_iso_cat_equivalence_equiv says that, for categories, isomorphisms of precategories are equivalent to equivalences.

quote: Since the type of functors between categories is 1-truncated, we conclude as well:
note: The lemma functor_type_groupoid says that WildFunctor C (D .wild) is a groupoid when D is a category. C is arbitrary.

quote: This result is one of the reasons that the primary objects of interest in category theory are the categories (i.e. univalent precategories), rather than the more general precategories.
note: This is a motivational remark without mathematical content.

quote: However, it's occasionally useful to present a category via a non-univalent precategory. This will not be equivalent to the corresponding category, so we need a notion that establishes their connection.
note: The literal reading ('will not be equivalent') can fail. The indiscrete precategory on Bool is not univalent, but it is equivalent to the terminal category. The intended reading is 'need not be equivalent', that is, a weak equivalence need not be an equivalence. A counterexample to that needs the failure of a choice principle. Thus it is not provable here (it is consistent with choice).

quote: From the point of view of categories, however, weak equivalences are as good as equivalences.
note: The result lem:precomp-equiv-cat (precomposition_cat_equivalence) makes this precise. For domains that are categories, thm:ff-eso-equiv also makes it precise.

quote: Our goal now is to construct for every precategory C a category L(C) along with a weak equivalence η : C → L(C). Here, L(C) is called the Rezk completion of C.
note: This is formalized in module 673.

quote: The idea is a generalization of the Cayley's lem:allgpsarepermutationgps, which is also how we'll go from abstract groups to concrete groups in ch:absgroup.
note: This is reading guidance and a forward reference. It makes no mathematical claim.

quote: Note that $\Set$ is a category, and hence so is the functor category $\Set^{\mathcal C\op}$ by~\cref{xca:functor-cat-univalent}.
note: Set is SetCat, the category of all sets of Narya's single universe (the book's Set_U). The presheaf category is a category by functor_wild_univalent (module 621) (xca:functor-cat-univalent).

quote: From~\cref{cor:yo-ff} we know that the Yoneda embedding $\yo : \mathcal C \to \Set^{\mathcal C\op}$ is fully faithful, motivating the following definition.
note: This is cor:yo-ff from module 622. The formalization uses it for rezk_unit_ff.

quote: We have that $\eta$ is fully faithful since $\yo$ is, and it's essentially surjective by definition.
note: The lemma rezk_unit_ff is literally yoneda_fully_faithful, because the hom-sets of the full subcategory are those of Set^{C^op}. The lemma rezk_unit_eso returns the membership proof of the object.

quote: Suppose now that $\mathcal C$ is essentially $\UU$-small, meaning that the type of objects $\Ob(\mathcal C)$ and all hom-sets are essentially $\UU$-small.
note: In the smallness-predicate model, this is equivalent to IsSmallWildPrecat of rem:cat-sizes (module 606). In that model, essential smallness and smallness agree.

quote: Then we have the hom-functor $\hom_{\mathcal C} : \mathcal C\op \times \mathcal C \to \Set_\UU$, so we get a Yoneda embedding $\mathcal C \to \Set_\UU^{\mathcal C\op}$.
note: Narya has one universe, so the presheaf category is valued in all sets. We record that the representable presheaves take U-small values when C is locally U-small. The two-variable hom-functor on C^op × C is not defined separately.

quote: Since $\Ob(\mathcal C)$ is essentially $\UU$-small, then $\Set_\UU^{\mathcal C\op}$ is locally $\UU$-small, and hence so is $L(\mathcal C)$.
note: The lemma presheaf_hom_essentially_small says this. Let C be essentially U-small. Then the natural transformations between presheaves on C with U-small values form an essentially U-small type. This is the statement that the book's Set_U^{C^op} is locally U-small. Via Yoneda, L(C) is locally U-small even without a smallness hypothesis on Ob(C).

quote: And now $\Ob(L(\mathcal C))$ is the image of $\Ob(\yo) : \Ob(\mathcal C) \to \Ob(\Set_\UU^{\mathcal C\op})$, which is then essentially $\UU$-small by the Replacement~\cref{pri:replacement}.
note: The lemma rezk_objects_image_equiv gives Ob(L(C)) ≃ Image(Ob(yo)). By the univalence of Set^{C^op}, mere isomorphisms are mere identifications. Our Ob(Set^{C^op}) is not locally U-small. Thus Replacement is applied to the surjection Ob(η) : Ob(C) → Ob(L(C)). Its codomain is locally U-small, because it is univalent with U-small hom-sets.

quote: even though $\Set_\UU^{\mathcal C\op}$ is only locally $\UU$-small when $\mathcal C$ is essentially $\UU$-small
note: The 'only when' direction is a cited theorem of Freyd and Street: if Set_U^{C^op} is locally small, then C is essentially small. It is not formalized. The 'when' direction is presheaf_hom_essentially_small.

quote: Another consequence of~\cref{cor:Cat-ua} is the following.
note: This is about the organisation of the proof. Our proof of the second part of thm:1types-are-groupoids uses the identity of (pre)categories (precategory_path_equiv, category_path_precat_equiv). The first part needs only path induction.

quote: [A,B] \jdeq \sum_{f : A \to B} \sum_{g : \prod_{x,y:A}(x\eqto y) \to (f(x) \eqto f(y))} \biggl(\prod_{x:A} g(\refl x) = \refl{f(x)}\biggr) \times \biggl(\prod_{x,y,z:A}\prod_{p:x\eqto y}\prod_{q:y\eqto z} g(qp) = g(q)g(p)\biggr)
note: The formalization gives an equivalence whose round trips are reflexivities (eta for records), in place of the judgmental equality. In PathWild, qp is p · q.

quote: Here, the two bracketed components are propositions.
note: This requires B to be a 1-type. Then the hom-sets of the path groupoid of B are sets.

quote: By path induction, $g$ is determined by its action on reflexivity, so the first bracketed component nails it down, so only the first component, the function $f:A\to B$, remains up to equivalence.
note: The lemma path_family_refl_equiv gives (Π x y, (x = y) → P x y) ≃ Π x, P x x by evaluation at refl. The lemma path_functor_action_contractible says that the pairs (g, identity law) are contractible with the centre ap f. The lemma path_groupoid_functors_equiv gives [A, B] ≃ (A → B).

quote: As a first consequence, the projection from the type of equivalences of groupoids, $A \equivto B$, to the type of equivalences of types, confusingly also denoted $A \equivto B$, is an equivalence. (Hence the confusion is harmless.)
note: Let A, B be 1-types. Then (F, E) ↦ (F₀, F₀ is an equivalence) is a BookIsEquiv CatEquivalence(PathWild A, PathWild B) → Equiv A B. The inverse sends e to the path functor of e. This functor is fully faithful because it is ap of an equivalence. Thus it is an equivalence by thm:ff-eso-equiv. The parenthetical remark is informal.

quote: This shows that $\UU^{\le 1} \to \Gpd$ is injective, so by~\cref{lem:inj+surj}, it remains to show it is surjective.
note: We construct the inverse G ↦ Ob(G) directly. Then we derive injectivity and surjectivity from the resulting equivalence. We do not go in the reverse direction.

quote: Observe that for a groupoid, the hom-sets and the identity arrows are determined by the univalence condition.
note: In a groupoid, (x = y) ≃ (x ≅ y) ≃ hom(x, y), and idtoiso(refl) = id. The map that forgets invertibility is an equivalence, because isIso is a contractible proposition.

quote: And relative to this, the composition operation is determined (by path induction) by its values at $\refl{y}p$, for all $p:x\eqto y$. But these values are forced to be $p$ by the left unit law.
note: The lemma cat_idtoiso_concat (module 626) proves idtoiso(p · q) = idtoiso(q) ∘ idtoiso(p). The proof is by path induction on q and uses the left unit law. This lemma is the composition law of the comparison functor.

quote: This identifies any groupoid with the path groupoid on its objects, showing that $\UU^{\le 1} \to \Gpd$ is surjective.
note: The formalization gives an isomorphism of precategories from the path groupoid of Ob(G) to G. It turns this isomorphism into an identification in Gpd via precategory_path_equiv (module 645).

quote: Can we think of them just in terms of categories? It turns out we can.
note: This is motivation. The precise content is thm:flagged-cat-equiv.

quote: The idea is that any precategory $\mathcal C$ presents a category $L(\mathcal C)$, its Rezk completion, but it has more structure, namely its type of objects, $\Ob(\mathcal C)$, as well as the relation between these and those of $L(\mathcal C)$, given by the functor $\eta : \mathcal C \to L(\mathcal C)$.
note: The structure is packaged as rezk_flag C = (L(C), Ob(C), Ob(η), surjectivity).

quote: Since $\eta$ is fully faithful, this structure boils down to the map on objects, $\Ob(\eta) : \Ob(\mathcal C) \to \Ob(L(\mathcal C))$.
note: C is recovered (up to identification of precategories) as the pullback of L(C) along Ob(η).

quote: The terminology is a bit whimsical: it's meant to indicate that we have a fat ``flag'' object, the category $\mathcal C$, equipped with a thinner ``flagpole'' object, the (higher) groupoid $A$, connected by the function $f$
note: This is an explanation of terminology with a picture.

quote: The flagged categories describe the fibers of the Rezk completion.
note: The fibre of L : Precat → Category at D is equivalent to FlagStructure D.

quote: We conclude that the following triangle commutes definitionally, displaying the fiber of Rezk completion at a category $\mathcal C$ as the type $\sum_{A:\UU}\sum_{f:A\to\Ob(\mathcal C)}\issurj(f)$
note: The equation fst ∘ F = L holds by refl. The fibre statement uses that F is an equivalence. It contracts the path component of the fibre of fst.

quote: The inverse at a triple $(\mathcal C,A,f)$ ``pulls back'' the (pre)category structure $\mathcal C$ along $f$ to get a precategory $\mathcal A$ on the object type $A$ and $\hom(x,y) \defeq \hom_{\mathcal C}(f(x), f(y))$, and likewise using $f$ to define identity arrows, composition, as well as unit and associativity laws.
note: Litmus tests: the pullback along the identity of Ob(D) gives D by refl. The pullback of Set along ★ ↦ Bool gives the endomaps of Bool.

quote: By construction, this extends $f$ to a fully faithful functor $f : \mathcal A \to \mathcal C$.
note: The functor is f on objects and the identity on arrows.

quote: This is also essentially surjective by the surjectivity of $f$, hence inducing an equivalence $L(\mathcal A) \equivto \mathcal C$.
note: Let F : C → D be a weak equivalence into a category. Then the restricted Yoneda functor d ↦ hom_D(F -, d) is an equivalence D ≃ L(C) that sends F(c) to η(c) (module 674). This gives the identification D = L(A) that flagged_round_trip uses.

quote: For the other round trip, starting with a precategory $\mathcal C$, we use the fully faithfulness of $\eta : \mathcal C \to L(\mathcal C)$ to identify the precategory structure on $\Ob(\mathcal C)$ with that pulled back from $L(\mathcal C)$.
note: The functor that is the identity on objects and yo on arrows is an isomorphism of precategories C ≅ Ob(η)*L(C). Thus it gives an identification (module 645).

quote: We have also seen two instances of limits and colimits, namely terminal and initial objects
note: The book does not define general limits and colimits. The section treats only products, coproducts and pullbacks. Thus the claim has no formal content here.

quote: We immediately recognize the product of types $A\times B$, along with the first and second projections, as a product cone $(A\times B,\fst,snd)$ in the wild category of types.
note: The factorizations of a cone (X, x₁, x₂) through A × B form a retract of a based path space. Thus they are contractible.

quote: Likewise, in the category of groups, the product G×H from ex:productofgroups forms a product cone when equipped with the projection homomorphisms.
note: The formalization proves IsProductCone (GroupCat .wild) G H (product_group G H, (product_group_proj1, product_group_proj2)) in the sense of def:prod-in-a-cat (module 665). The map f ↦ (p1 ∘ f, p2 ∘ f) : Hom(K, G × H) → Hom(K, G) × Hom(K, H) is an equivalence. Its inverse pairs the classifying maps and the pointing paths. The factorizations of a cone are its book fiber. Hence GroupCat has binary products. By univalence, every product cone on G, H equals this one. Litmus test: the cone (Σ_3, id, id) factors through the diagonal x ↦ (x, x) (refl).

quote: We say that a (wild) category \emph{has binary products} if every pair of objects $A,B$ as a product cone.
note: HasBinaryProducts C ≔ (a b : C .ob) → ProductCone C a b. For a univalent C, it is a proposition. The word 'as' in the book is a typo for 'has'.

quote: In this case we are justified by~\cref{xca:product-cone-prop} in writing $(A\times B,\fst,\snd)$ for the (unique) product cone on $A,B$.
note: In a univalent wild precategory, a given product cone makes the type of product cones contractible. In the wild category of types, every product cone equals (A × B, fst, snd).

quote: Like every categorical notion, there is of course a dual notion, obtained by turning all the arrows around.
note: The relation to products is as follows. IsCoproductCocone C a b K is by refl IsProductCone (OppositeWild C) a b K. The cocone precategory is the opposite of the cone precategory of C^op.

quote: In other words, a coproduct cocone is an initial cocone under the pair of objects $A,B$.
note: For C with hom-sets, this holds by refl. IsCoproductCocone C a b K is the statement that every hom type out of K in the cocone precategory is contractible. This is def:initial-obj, unfolded.

quote: In the wild category of types, we have the coproduct cocones $(A \coprod B, \inl{}, \inr{})$.
note: Precomposition with inl, inr is an equivalence (A ⊔ B → X) ≃ (A → X) × (B → X). The factorizations of a cocone are a retract of its book fiber.

quote: We haven't yet seen the coproduct of groups; knowing about products and categorical duality, we'd be bound to discover them! We shall study them in sec:coprod.
note: This is a forward reference without a claim that can be checked. The book constructs and studies the coproduct of groups in sec:coprod (chapter 8, congp.tex, module range 800–899). It needs pushouts of classifying types, and chapter 6 does not provide them. The coproduct cocones of types in the same sentence belong to def:coprod-in-a-cat (module 665).

quote: Let's look at another pair of examples: pullbacks and pushouts.
note: This chapter does not define pushouts. Module 666 formalizes pullbacks of types.

quote: the ``pullback'' which we will now define should be thought about as the type of all pairs of elements $(b,c):B\times C$ so that $f(b)\eqto g(c)$.
note: This agrees with def:pullback: TypePullback B C D f g ≔ Σ_{(b,c)} f(b) = g(c).

quote: This construction is important in many situations also beyond group theory.
note: This is motivation.

quote: In view of \cref{xca:univpropofpullback} we will say that we have a \emph{pullback diagram} [...] to indicate that we have an element in $(A\to B)\times_{(A\to D)}(A\to C)$ such that the resulting map $A\to B\times_DC$ is an equivalence.
note: IsPullbackSquare A B C D f g w ≔ BookIsEquiv of the gap map a ↦ (β(a), γ(a), happly p a). As checks, the formalization shows that the defining square of B ×_D C and the preimage square of the example are pullback diagrams.

quote: This is emphasized with the little $\lrcorner$ symbol in the upper left corner.
note: This is diagram notation.

quote: \section{Monoidal categories}
note: The section is empty in the pinned book. Only LaTeX comments follow. There is nothing to formalize.

quote: In this chapter we will implement an inverse construction, how to obtain a (concrete) group from an abstract one
note: The construction concr (module 707) is the group that the abstract torsors classify. Module 709 proves both round trips. Thus abstr : Group → AbstractGroup is an equivalence with inverse concr.

quote: we show how to obtain a (concrete) homomorphism from an abstract one
note: The function deloop_hom (module 710) reconstructs a homomorphism G → H from an abstract homomorphism abstr G → abstr H (lem:homomabstrconcr). The function concr_hom (module 742) is concr on morphisms.

quote: Of course this is not a reason to stop here, but to continue finding out which parts of group theory benefit from the concrete approach.
note: This footnote gives motivation. It contains no mathematical claim.

quote: More precisely, we give an equivalence of categories between the categories of concrete and of abstract groups.
note: This is thm:concr-equiv-cats, module 744, with the wild precategories GroupWild (chapter 6) and AbstractGroupWild.

quote: One could advocate for the name `abstract monoid' here, were it not the case that we have no concrete analogue for monoids in our setting. The reason is the symmetry of the identity types.
note: This footnote is about terminology. The reason that it gives is informal: identity types are symmetric, so loop spaces are groups.

quote: A monoid is a collection of data consisting only of \ref{struc:under-set}, \ref{struc:unit}, and \ref{struc:mult-op} from the list in \cref{def:abstractgroup}. In other words, the existence of inverses is not assumed.
note: Monoid (module 700) has the underlying set, the unit and the multiplication, with the monoid laws. The map abstract_group_monoid forgets the inverse operation of an abstract group. Examples of monoids without inverses are list_monoid_no_inverse (module 720) and two_element_monoid_no_inverse (module 728).

quote: Building on the definition of a monoid, we may encode the type of abstract groups as follows. [...] Using that notation, we introduce names for the relevant propositions. UnitLaws(S,e,μ) :≡ ..., AssocLaw(S,μ) :≡ ..., MonoidLaws(S,e,μ) :≡ isSet(S) × UnitLaws × AssocLaw, InverseLaw(S,e,μ,ι) :≡ ..., GroupLaws(S,e,μ,ι) :≡ MonoidLaws × InverseLaw
note: Module 700 defines the named laws as displayed (products nested to the right). They are propositions: monoid_laws_prop and group_laws_prop (isSet S is part of MonoidLaws), and inverse_law_prop (module 721). The equivalence group_laws_equiv identifies GroupLaws with the laws record of module 403.

quote: an abstract group $\mathscr G$ will be a quintuple of the form $\mathscr G \jdeq (S,e,\mu,\iota,!)$. For brevity, we will usually omit the proof of the properties from the display, since it's unique, and write an abstract group as though it were a quadruple
note: The quintuple form is AbstractGroupSigma. It is equivalent to the record AbstractGroup, with refl round trips (abstract_group_sigma_equiv). The uniqueness of the proof of the laws is group_laws_prop / abstract_group_laws_prop. The lemmas abstract_group_laws_irrelevant (module 430) and abstract_group_path_of_data (module 702) show that the quadruple (S, e, μ, ι) determines the abstract group.

quote: In this section we define the notion of homomorphism for abstract groups, which we touched upon in~\cref{rem:first-abs-hom}. We start by an exercise that simplifies the requirements for abstract group homomorphisms.
note: This is a section overview without a mathematical claim. The notion is IsAbstractHom / AbstractHom (module 403), and the exercise is xca:onlymult-hom.

quote: Thus we see that, due to the properties of the abstract groups, if $f$ preserves multiplication, then $f$ also preserves unit and inverses.
note: This is xca:onlymult-hom (module 701). The lemma abstract_hom_monoid_hom packages the unit equation into a monoid homomorphism.

quote: For monoids this is not true: Let $M$ be the monoid with two elements, $1$ and $0$, with ordinary multiplication, so the unit is $1$. Consider $\bn1$ as the trivial monoid. Now define $h: \bn1\to M$ by $h(0)=0$. Then $h$ preserves multiplication, but not the unit.
note: Module 728: M is Bool with 0 = false, 1 = true, x·y = x ∧ y and unit true (two_element_monoid). The trivial monoid is unit_monoid on Unit. The map h = monoid_footnote_map (constant false) preserves multiplication by refl. The formalization refutes h(*) = 1. Thus h is not a MonoidHom, and the monoid analogue of xca:onlymult-hom fails (monoid_mul_preserving_not_unit_preserving).

quote: Note that $M$ cannot be extended to an abstract group, since giving $0$ an inverse would make $0$ equal to $1$.
note: An inverse x of 0 gives 0 = 0·x = 1 (two_element_monoid_zero_inverse, whose conclusion is Id Bool false true). Thus M has no inverse operation with the law of inverses, and not even mere inverses. No abstract group has M as its underlying monoid (two_element_monoid_not_abstract_group, module 728).

quote: it will then be relatively simple to show that the constructions of forming the abstract group of a group and taking the group classified by the torsors of an abstract group are inverse to each other.
note: Module 709.

quote: Then we can view $X$ as the classifying function of a group homomorphism from $G$ to $\SG_{X(\sh_G)}$.
note: Chapter 5 (rem:GSet=SetHomG, module 560) gives GSet G ≃ Σ_S GroupActionOnSet G S with GroupActionOnSet G S = GroupHom G (permutation_group S). The restriction of the codomain to the component is ptd_conn_to_comp_equiv.

quote: Its underlying set is $\USymG$. The abstract version of the corresponding homomorphism, defined by transport, is the function $\USymG\to(\USymG\eqto\USymG)$ mapping $g$ to $(g\cdot\blank)$, \ie postcomposition with $g$.
note: The principal abstr(G)-torsor acts by g · h = concat h g (left multiplication / postcomposition with g), by refl (agset_principal_abstr_act). For z ≡ sh_G, the abstr(G)-set of ex:BqG is the principal torsor (bq_gset_principal).

quote: A (free) choice has been made to define $\princ G$ using $(\sh_G\eqto z)$ and not $(z\eqto\sh_G)$. In the latter case the abstract homomorphism would map $g$ to $(\blank\cdot\inv g)$, \ie precomposition with the inverse of $g$.
note: Module 712 gives the abstr(G)-set (sh_G = z, r ↦ r g⁻¹) and its identification with the principal torsor at z ≡ sh_G (through xca:absprtorsor).

quote: Clearly, the types $\absGSet$ and $\absGTor$ are groupoids, and the latter is by definition connected.
note: Modules 706–707. The proof of agset_groupoid uses the identification of paths of G-sets with isomorphisms (agset_path_iso_equiv).

quote: We recognize $\preinv$ from \cref{lem:pathsptransportiseq} as the induced map of identity types ... followed by evaluation at $z$. Post-composition $\post$ is transport in the family $\pathsp x$, while $\preinv$ is precomposition by the inverse of its argument.

note: This is the instance H = permutation_group S of abstr_hom_equiv G H (module 710). The formalization uses it fibrewise in ev_gset_chain_equiv.

note: The equivalence ev_gset_chain_equiv is gset_action_equiv, followed by family_equiv of abstr_hom_equiv. The last step is a judgmental equality of types (ev_gset_chain_last_step, refl).

quote: Backtracking these equivalences we see that we have established
note: The composite of the chain is ev_{sh_G} by refl (ev_gset_chain_map). Thus gset_abstract_gset_equiv has the map ev_gset.

quote: Recall from \cref{sec:phi-functors} the adjoint triple $\varphi_!\dashv\varphi^*\dashv\varphi_*$ for a given abstract homomorphism $\varphi$. ... Also recall the adjoint triple $f_!\dashv f^*\dashv f_*$ from \cref{def:restrictandinduce,rem:coinduced-Hset}.
note: This recalls results that are proved elsewhere. The concrete adjunctions are in module 542. The abstract ones are in our sec:phi-functors modules (740 and the adjunction modules).

quote: Since $f^*$ and $\abstr(f)^*$ are both defined by precomposition, the following diagram can easily be filled
note: The filler of the square is restrict_ev_square (xca:f^*-abs(f)^*). In addition to precomposition, the filler needs transport along the pointing path Bf_pt, because Y(Bf(sh_G)) and Y(sh_H) are different sets.
